115961.m: Star signs and constellations no longer match today.

115962.q: Why do many people find their horoscope surprisingly accurate?
a: The statements are so general that they fit almost everyone
Horoscopes are measured for each person individually
115962.e: Sentences like “You are sometimes unsure of yourself” fit almost everyone. In an experiment, most students found the same text very accurate as their very own personal profile.
115962.m: General statements often seem surprisingly personal.

115963.q: What do scientific tests show in which astrologers have to match horoscopes to the right people?
a: Their hits are no better than chance
They are only right with children
They are only right at full moon
115963.e: In such blind tests, the astrologers do not know whose horoscope is whose. They are not right more often than by pure guessing.
115963.m: In controlled tests, astrology predicts no more than chance.

115964.q: What does a horoscope originally show?
a: The positions of the heavenly bodies at a point in time
The weather forecast for a week
The Sun's path around the Earth
115964.e: A horoscope is a drawing that records the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets, for example at birth. Astrology interprets character and fate from it.
115964.m: A horoscope shows the sky at a particular moment.

115965.q: Which famous astronomer also made horoscopes to earn money?
115965.e: Kepler discovered the laws of planetary orbits. Because horoscopes were in demand at the time, he also wrote them and partly paid his living costs that way.
115965.m: Even great astronomers used to write horoscopes for money.

115966.q: What do people want to find with a dowsing rod?
115966.e: Traditionally, people use a dowsing rod to search for underground water, ores or supposed “earth rays”.
115966.m: A dowsing rod is mainly used to search for water.

115967.q: What shape is a classic dowsing rod?
115967.e: The rod is held at both ends with tense hands. Modern rods are often bent wires or metal rods too.
115967.m: The classic dowsing rod is a forked branch.

115968.q: What are people called who search with a dowsing rod?
115968.e: Dowsers walk slowly across an area and watch for the rod to move. There is no scientifically recognised training for this.
115968.m: Someone who searches with a dowsing rod is called a dowser.

115969.q: What best explains why a dowsing rod moves?
115969.e: In the ideomotor effect, the muscles move very slightly without you noticing. The tense rod amplifies these small movements into a clear swing.
115969.m: The rod moves because of unconscious hand movements.

115970.q: Why do dowsers often seem successful when looking for water?
a: In many areas you find groundwater almost everywhere
115970.e: In central Europe, in many areas there is groundwater almost everywhere at a certain depth. A hit therefore does not prove that the rod works.
115970.m: Hits are no proof if you find water almost everywhere.

115971.q: How does groundwater usually occur in the ground?
a: In huge cave lakes under every town
115971.e: Groundwater usually fills the pores and cracks of gravel, sand or rock over large areas. Narrow “water veins”, as dowsers describe them, are the exception.
115971.m: Groundwater usually lies in wide layers, not narrow veins.

115972.q: How can you fairly test whether a person finds water with a dowsing rod?
a: With a blind test using hidden water pipes
115972.e: In a blind test, neither the person nor the observer knows which hidden pipe water is flowing through. Only this shows whether the hit rate is above chance.
115972.m: Only blind tests show whether an ability really exists.

115973.q: What happened to the one million dollar prize that the James Randi Educational Foundation offered for proof of supernatural abilities?
115973.e: Many applicants, including dowsers, came to be tested. None could show their ability under controlled conditions.
115973.m: Under controlled conditions, nobody could prove supernatural powers.

115974.q: Looked at closely, what shape is the Earth?
a: A sphere slightly flattened at the poles
115974.e: Because it spins, the Earth is a little wider at the equator than from pole to pole. The difference between the diameters is about 43 km.
115974.m: The Earth is slightly flattened at the poles.

115975.q: Which observation did Aristotle give as a sign that the Earth is round?
a: The round shadow of the Earth during lunar eclipses
115975.e: In a lunar eclipse, the Earth's shadow falls on the moon and is always round. Only a sphere casts a round shadow from every direction.
115975.m: The Earth's round shadow on the moon reveals its shape.

115976.q: What do you see when a ship at sea sails far away?
a: It disappears from the bottom up
It just gets smaller and smaller
It disappears from the top down
115976.e: Because of the Earth's curve, the hull disappears behind the horizon first and the top of the mast last. On a flat Earth, the ship would simply get smaller.
115976.m: Because of the Earth's curve, ships disappear from the bottom first.

115977.q: Is it true that scholars in the Middle Ages thought the Earth was a disc?
a: No, they knew it was round
Yes, they all thought it was flat
No, they thought it was a cube
115977.e: Since ancient times, educated people knew the Earth was a sphere. The idea that the Middle Ages believed in a disc is itself a myth from later times.
115977.m: Medieval scholars knew that the Earth is a sphere.

115978.q: What was the argument before Columbus's voyage in 1492 really about?
115978.e: Columbus thought the Earth was far too small and the route to Asia too short. His critics were right that Asia was too far away.
115978.m: Columbus was wrong about the size of the Earth, not its shape.

115979.q: Which expedition was the first to sail around the whole world, from 1519 to 1522?
115979.e: Ferdinand Magellan died on the way, but Juan Sebastián Elcano completed the voyage with one ship. The journey around the world confirmed in practice that the Earth is round.
115979.m: Magellan's expedition was the first to sail around the Earth.

115980.q: Why is it still early morning in New York when it is already midday in Zurich?
a: Because the Sun only lights up half of the spinning globe
Because New York is higher up
Because the clocks in the USA are wrong
Because the Sun is closer in Europe
115980.e: The Earth spins, and only one half of the globe faces the Sun at any time. That is why there are time zones, which could not be explained on a flat disc.
115980.m: Time zones exist because the Earth spins.

115981.q: Roughly how long is the Earth's circumference at the equator?
115981.e: The circumference at the equator is about 40,075 km. The metre was originally defined so that a quarter of a meridian is 10,000 km long.
115981.m: The Earth measures about 40,000 km around the equator.

115982.q: What do astronauts see from the ISS space station at a height of about 400 km?
a: The curved surface of the Earth
A wall of ice around the world
115982.e: From the ISS the horizon is clearly curved. The station circles the Earth about every 90 minutes.
115982.m: From space you can clearly see that the Earth is round.

115983.q: What do you do in a fact check?
a: You check whether a claim is true
115983.e: In a fact check, statements are compared with reliable sources and data. The result can be true, false or misleading.
115983.m: A fact check tests claims against evidence.

115984.q: How can you find out where and when a photo first appeared on the internet?
115984.e: In a reverse search, you upload the image to a search engine. This shows whether an old image is being spread again in the wrong context.
115984.m: A reverse image search shows where a photo comes from.

115985.q: A supposed quote from a famous person goes viral. What is a sensible step to check it?
a: Look for the original source of the quote
Look at the number of likes
115985.e: Many quotes are falsely put into the mouths of famous people. Only a book, speech or interview as a source shows whether someone really said it.
115985.m: A quote is only believable once you know its source.

115986.q: What is the best way to check an unfamiliar website?
a: Read what other sources say about it
See whether it is nicely designed
Believe it if it is at the top of the search results
115986.e: Instead of just staying on the site, you look in other tabs to see who is behind it. Professional fact-checkers work this way too.
115986.m: It is best to check a source from the outside.

115987.q: Which hidden information in a photo file can reveal when and with what a picture was taken?
115987.e: Cameras and phones often store the date, the device and sometimes the location in the file. But this metadata can also be missing or changed.
115987.m: Metadata reveals a lot about where a photo comes from.

115988.q: A risk rises from 1 to 2 cases per 10,000 people. By how much has the risk risen in absolute terms?
115988.e: 1 in 10,000 is 0.01 per cent, 2 in 10,000 is 0.02 per cent. So the rise is only 0.01 percentage points, even though the risk has “doubled”.
115988.m: Doubling can mean very little with small numbers.

115989.q: In summer, ice cream sales and swimming accidents rise at the same time. What follows from this?
a: Both have a common cause, the heat
Swimming accidents make you want ice cream
115989.e: Two things that rise together are not necessarily cause and effect. Here, the warm weather leads to more ice cream and more swimmers.
115989.m: Rising together does not prove a cause.

115990.q: Why should you read more than just the headline before sharing an article?
115990.e: A headline has to be short and eye-catching, so it often leaves out important things. Only the whole text shows what is really being claimed.
115990.m: Read the whole article before sharing it.

a: Checking the origin and credibility of a source
Rating a source as badly as possible
115991.e: In source criticism, you ask who wrote something, when, where and with what intention. Only then can you judge how reliable a piece of information is.
115991.m: Source criticism means checking where information comes from.

115992.q: A diary from 1940 is read in a history lesson. What kind of source is it?
115992.e: Primary sources come directly from the time being studied. A school book that reports on that time would be a secondary source.
115992.m: Primary sources come from the time in question.

115993.q: Where on a website do you find who is responsible for the content?
115993.e: Serious websites give the names and contact details of those responsible in the legal notice. If there is none, be careful.
115993.m: The legal notice shows who is behind a website.

115994.q: What is the best way to check a statement in a Wikipedia article?
115994.e: Wikipedia articles are supposed to back up their statements with evidence. The references lead you to the original source.
115994.m: On Wikipedia, it is worth looking at the references.

115995.q: What does the label “Ad” or “Sponsored” on a post mean?
115995.e: Such posts were paid for by a company. They are mainly meant to sell and are therefore not neutral.
115995.m: Sponsored posts are adverts and not neutral.

115996.q: A study on sugary drinks was paid for by a drinks maker. What should you pay special attention to?
115996.e: Whoever pays for a study often has an interest in a particular result. The study is not automatically wrong, but it should be checked especially carefully.
115996.m: With paid-for studies, check for conflicts of interest.

115997.q: Why is the publication date of a source important?
a: Older information can be out of date
115997.e: Figures, records or research results change over time. An old article may therefore no longer be true today.
115997.m: With every source, check how up to date it is.

115998.q: Which question is NOT one of the typical questions of source criticism?
a: How many likes does the post have?
With what intention was it made?
115998.e: The number of likes only shows how popular a post is, not whether it is true. What matters is the author, the time and the intention.

a: Checking of a study by independent experts
A rating in the app store
115999.e: Before a journal publishes a study, other experts read it critically. They look for mistakes and often ask for improvements.
115999.m: In peer review, experts check the work of other experts.

116000.q: What does the word “peer” mean in peer review?
116000.e: The reviewers are researchers from the same field. So they are “equals” of the authors.
116000.m: Peers are experts at the same level.

116001.q: What does double-blind peer review mean?
a: Reviewers and researchers do not know each other's names
The study is checked in the dark
116001.e: This is so that fame, friendship or rivalry does not influence the judgement. Only the work itself is assessed.
116001.m: In double-blind peer review, both sides stay anonymous.

116002.e: Preprints make results available quickly, for example during a crisis. But they have not yet been checked by experts, so they should be read with caution.
116002.m: Preprints are studies that have not yet been reviewed.

116003.q: What can peer review NOT guarantee?
a: That a result is definitely correct
116003.e: Reviewers only see the submitted manuscript and cannot repeat every experiment. Mistakes or even fraud can therefore go undetected.
116003.m: Peer review reduces mistakes, but does not make results infallible.

116004.q: What is it called when other researchers repeat an experiment to check the result?
116004.e: A result is considered especially reliable if independent teams confirm it several times. If it cannot be repeated, caution is needed.
116004.m: Repeated experiments make knowledge more certain.

116005.q: What happens to a published study if serious mistakes or deception are found later?
116005.e: In 2010, for example, the journal “The Lancet” withdrew a 1998 study that had claimed a false link between vaccination and autism.

116006.q: Which journal is a well-known example of a peer-reviewed journal?
116006.e: “Nature” has been published since 1869 and publishes research from all the natural sciences. Submitted papers are reviewed by experts.
116006.m: Major journals have studies checked before they are printed.

116007.q: What are publishers called that publish almost anything for payment without real review?
116007.e: Predatory publishers pretend to be serious academic journals but hardly check the papers. Their articles are therefore less trustworthy.
116007.m: Not every journal with a scientific name really checks.

116008.q: From which subunits does filamentous F-actin in muscle polymerise?
116008.e: F-actin forms when many globular G-actin molecules join together. The G stands for globular, the F for filamentous.
116008.m: Many globular G-actins together form an F-actin filament.

116009.q: Which thread-like protein lies in the groove of the actin filament and covers the binding sites for myosin at rest?
116009.e: Tropomyosin winds along the actin filament and blocks the myosin binding sites at rest. Only when calcium binds to troponin is it moved aside.
116009.m: At rest, tropomyosin blocks myosin's access to actin.

116010.q: Which ions must be released in the muscle cell for the muscle to contract?
116010.e: Calcium binds to troponin. This moves tropomyosin aside, and myosin can attach to actin.

116011.q: What is the smallest contractile unit of a muscle fibre, bounded by two Z discs, called?
116011.e: In the sarcomere, actin and myosin filaments are arranged regularly. When it contracts they slide past each other and the Z discs move closer together.
116011.m: The sarcomere is the smallest working unit of the muscle.

116012.q: Which protein forms the thick filaments in muscle that pull on the actin filaments?
116012.e: The heads of myosin bind to actin and, using ATP, pull it towards the middle of the sarcomere. This shortens the muscle.
116012.m: Myosin pulls on actin and so shortens the muscle.

116013.q: What is the explanation of muscle contraction called in which actin and myosin filaments slide past each other?
116013.e: The filaments themselves do not get shorter. They slide into each other, which shortens each sarcomere and so the whole muscle.
116013.m: During contraction, actin and myosin slide past each other.

116014.q: To which component of all body cells do actin filaments also belong outside muscle?
116014.e: As microfilaments, actin threads form part of the cytoskeleton. They stabilise the shape of the cell and make cell movement possible.
116014.m: Actin occurs as microfilaments in practically all cells.

116015.q: What shape does an actin filament have?
a: Two chains twisted around each other
A flat band of folded sheets
116015.e: An actin filament looks like two twisted strings of beads. The hollow cylinder of 13 protofilaments, by contrast, describes a microtubule.
116015.m: An actin filament looks like two twisted strings of beads.

116016.q: Which part of the myosin II molecule has ATPase activity?
116016.e: The head of myosin binds both actin and ATP and splits the ATP. The long tail is used to assemble into thick filaments.
116016.m: The myosin head is both motor and ATP-splitting enzyme.

116017.q: How is a myosin II molecule in muscle built?
a: A long tail with two heads
A chain of spheres without a head
116017.e: Two myosin chains twist into a long tail and end in two heads. Many such molecules assemble into thick filaments.
116017.m: Myosin II has two heads on a long tail.

116018.q: Which substance supplies the energy for the movement of the myosin heads?
116018.e: The myosin head splits ATP and uses the energy released to cock itself. In the power stroke it pulls the actin filament a bit further.
116018.m: Myosin heads move with energy from ATP.

116019.q: Does myosin form the thick or the thin filaments in the sarcomere?
116019.e: Many myosin molecules form the thick filaments in the middle of the sarcomere. The thin filaments consist mainly of actin.
116019.m: Myosin forms the thick filaments, actin the thin ones.

116020.q: Why does rigor mortis set in after death?
a: Without ATP, the myosin heads stay stuck to the actin
The calcium is completely broken down
The actin breaks down into G-actin
The muscle fills with lactate crystals
116020.e: Without ATP the cross-bridges can no longer detach, so actin and myosin stay firmly linked. The stiffness only wears off when the proteins decompose.
116020.m: Rigor mortis is a result of missing ATP.

116021.q: What does the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction state?
a: The filaments slide past each other without getting shorter themselves
The filaments contract like rubber bands
The muscle fibres get shorter by taking up water
The filaments dissolve with every contraction
116021.e: In 1954 several researchers showed that actin and myosin filaments keep their length. The muscle shortens because they slide further into each other.
116021.m: During contraction the filaments slide into each other.

116022.q: In which direction do the myosin heads pull the actin filaments during contraction?
a: Towards the middle of the sarcomere
116022.e: The myosin heads on both sides of the M line pull the actin filaments towards the middle of the sarcomere. This brings the Z discs closer together.
116022.m: During contraction the actin filaments slide towards the middle of the sarcomere.

116023.q: What are the connections between myosin heads and actin that form in cycles during contraction called?
116023.e: The myosin heads form temporary cross-bridges with the actin. Each cycle of binding, tilting and releasing uses one ATP.
116023.m: Myosin and actin connect via cross-bridges.

116024.q: Which structures bound a sarcomere at both ends?
116024.e: A sarcomere runs from one Z disc to the next. It is the smallest contractile unit of striated muscle.
116024.m: A sarcomere lies between two Z discs.

116025.q: What is the light area of the sarcomere called that contains only thin actin filaments?
116025.e: The I band contains only actin filaments and appears light (isotropic) under a polarising microscope. It is cut in half by the Z disc.
116025.m: The I band contains only actin filaments.

116026.q: What is the central area of the sarcomere called where only myosin filaments lie, without overlap with actin?
116026.e: The H zone contains myosin filaments but no actin filaments. During contraction it becomes narrower or disappears completely.
116026.m: The H zone is the actin-free middle of the sarcomere.

116027.q: Which section of the sarcomere stays the same length during contraction?
a: The distance between the Z discs
116027.e: The A band matches the length of the myosin filaments, which do not shorten. The I band and H zone get shorter because the filaments overlap more.
116027.m: The A band keeps its length during contraction.

116028.q: Roughly how long is a sarcomere in resting skeletal muscle?
116028.e: A resting sarcomere measures about 2 to 2.5 micrometres. Thousands of sarcomeres in a row form a myofibril.
116028.m: A sarcomere is only a few micrometres long.

116029.q: Which protein of the sarcomere is considered the largest known human protein?
116029.e: Titin reaches from the Z disc to the M line and acts like an elastic spring. Depending on the variant, it consists of about 27,000 to over 34,000 amino acids.
116029.m: Titin is the giant protein and the spring of the sarcomere.

116030.q: At what sarcomere length does a skeletal muscle produce the greatest force?
a: At medium length with optimal overlap
The force does not depend on length
116030.e: The force depends on the number of possible cross-bridges. With optimal overlap of actin and myosin there are the most, with strong stretching or compression fewer.
116030.m: The greatest force comes with optimal filament overlap.

116031.q: What is the structure in the middle of the sarcomere called where the myosin filaments are anchored?
116031.e: In the M line, proteins such as myomesin link the thick filaments together. It lies exactly in the middle of the A band.
116031.m: The M line holds the myosin filaments together in the middle of the sarcomere.

116032.q: Why does skeletal muscle look striated under the microscope?
a: The sarcomeres lie regularly side by side
The cell nuclei lie in rows
Connective tissue wraps around the fibres
116032.e: In all myofibrils the sarcomeres lie at the same level. So light I bands and dark A bands form a continuous striped pattern.
116032.m: The striations come from the exact arrangement of the sarcomeres.

116033.q: What is a motor end plate?
a: The synapse between motor neuron and muscle fibre
The end of a tendon at the bone
The connection between two heart muscle cells
116033.e: At the motor end plate a motor neuron passes its signal chemically to a skeletal muscle fibre. It is also called the neuromuscular junction.
116033.m: The motor end plate is the synapse between nerve and muscle.

116034.q: Which enzyme quickly breaks down acetylcholine at the motor end plate?
116034.e: Acetylcholinesterase splits the messenger substance in the synaptic cleft within milliseconds. This stops the muscle staying permanently excited. Some nerve poisons inhibit this enzyme.
116034.m: Acetylcholinesterase ends the signal at the end plate.

116035.q: What happens at the muscle fibre membrane when acetylcholine binds to its receptors?
a: Ion channels open and the membrane is depolarised
The membrane becomes impermeable to all ions
The muscle fibre makes acetylcholine itself
116035.e: The receptors are also ion channels. Mainly sodium flows in, the voltage across the membrane flips and triggers an action potential.
116035.m: Acetylcholine opens ion channels and excites the muscle fibre.

116036.q: What does every end plate potential normally trigger in the skeletal muscle fibre?
116036.e: The end plate potential is so large that it reliably crosses the threshold. This is called a high safety factor of transmission.
116036.m: At a healthy end plate, every signal leads to an action potential.

116037.q: Which disease is caused by autoantibodies against the acetylcholine receptors of the motor end plate?
116037.e: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies block and destroy the receptors. Typical is muscle weakness that increases with use.
116037.m: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease of the end plate.

116038.q: How does the arrow poison curare act at the motor end plate?
a: It inhibits the breakdown of acetylcholine
It opens the calcium channels permanently
It increases the release of acetylcholine
116038.e: Curare occupies the receptors without opening them. The muscles become limp and paralysed, including the breathing muscles.
116038.m: Curare causes limp paralysis by blocking receptors.

116039.q: How does botulinum toxin act at the motor end plate?
a: It prevents the release of acetylcholine
116039.e: Botulinum toxin splits proteins needed for the vesicles to fuse with the membrane. Without the transmitter the muscle stays limp.

116040.q: Which ions flowing into the nerve ending trigger the release of the transmitter at the end plate?
116040.e: The arriving action potential opens voltage-gated calcium channels. The incoming calcium triggers the exocytosis of the vesicles.
116040.m: Calcium is the start signal for exocytosis of the transmitter vesicles.

116041.q: What is a motor neuron together with all the muscle fibres it supplies called?
116041.e: All fibres of a motor unit contract at the same time. In eye muscles there are only a few fibres, in large leg muscles often hundreds to over a thousand.
116041.m: A motor unit consists of one motor neuron and its muscle fibres.

116042.q: Which enzyme breaks down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft?
116042.e: Acetylcholinesterase splits acetylcholine into acetate and choline. This ends the excitation at the synapse very quickly.
116042.m: Acetylcholinesterase ends the action of acetylcholine.

116043.q: Where in the nerve cell is acetylcholine stored until it is released?
116043.e: Acetylcholine is packed into small vesicles in the nerve ending. When an action potential arrives, they fuse with the membrane and release the messenger into the cleft.
116043.m: Messenger substances are stored and released in vesicles.

116044.q: After the poison of which mushroom are the muscarinic acetylcholine receptors named?
116044.e: The poison muscarine was obtained from the fly agaric (Amanita muscaria) in 1869. It specifically activates one type of acetylcholine receptor, which is therefore called muscarinic.
116044.m: The muscarinic receptors are named after a fly agaric poison.

116045.q: What are substances such as acetylcholine called that carry signals at synapses from one nerve cell to the next?
116045.e: Neurotransmitters are released at the synapse and bind to receptors on the next cell. Acetylcholine was the first neurotransmitter to be discovered.

116046.q: What happens in poisoning with nerve agents that inhibit acetylcholinesterase?
a: Acetylcholine builds up and causes constant excitation
116046.e: Without breakdown, acetylcholine stays in the cleft and keeps exciting the receptors. Muscle twitching, cramps and finally paralysis follow.
116046.m: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors lead to constant excitation.

116047.q: At which junction does a nerve use acetylcholine to pass the command on to a skeletal muscle?
116047.e: At the motor end plate the nerve ending releases acetylcholine. It binds to receptors on the muscle fibre, which then contracts.
116047.m: At the motor end plate, acetylcholine controls the muscle.

116048.q: How does acetylcholine released by the vagus nerve change the heart rate?
116048.e: At the heart, acetylcholine acts through muscarinic receptors at the sinus node. In this way the parasympathetic nervous system slows the heartbeat.
116048.m: Acetylcholine from the vagus nerve slows the heart.

116049.q: What triggers the release of acetylcholine from the nerve ending?
a: The formation of new muscle fibres
A signal from the muscle's cell nucleus
116049.e: When an action potential reaches the nerve ending, calcium flows in. The vesicles then fuse with the membrane and release acetylcholine.
116049.m: An action potential triggers the release of the messenger substance.

116050.q: What building blocks make up an ATP molecule?
a: Adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups
Adenine, deoxyribose and two phosphate groups
Adenosine, glucose and three phosphate groups
Guanine, ribose and three phosphate groups
116050.e: ATP is a nucleotide made of the base adenine, the sugar ribose and three phosphate groups. The bonds between the phosphates are rich in energy.
116050.m: ATP consists of adenine, ribose and three phosphates.

116051.q: Under standard conditions, roughly how much free energy is released when ATP is hydrolysed to ADP and phosphate?
116051.e: The standard value is about minus 30.5 kJ per mole. In the cell the amount is even larger because of the concentrations.
116051.m: Splitting ATP releases about 30 kilojoules per mole.

116052.q: Roughly how long does the ATP stored in muscle last under maximum effort?
116052.e: Muscle stores only very little ATP directly. That is why it has to be constantly remade from creatine phosphate, glucose and fats.
116052.m: The muscle's direct ATP store is very small.

116053.q: In which organelles of the muscle fibre is most ATP made during aerobic energy production?
116053.e: The citric acid cycle and the respiratory chain take place in the mitochondria. Endurance-trained muscles have especially many mitochondria.
116053.m: Mitochondria are the power stations of the muscle cell.

116054.q: How many ATP molecules does anaerobic glycolysis yield net per molecule of glucose?
116054.e: Glycolysis produces 4 ATP, but 2 are used up at the start. That leaves a net 2 ATP per glucose.
116054.m: Glycolysis yields a net two ATP per glucose.

116055.q: Roughly how much ATP does an adult turn over per day?
116055.e: Because ATP is constantly split and rebuilt, the turnover adds up to dozens of kilograms per day. Only a small amount is present in the body at any time.
116055.m: ATP is recycled many thousands of times a day.

116056.q: Which substance in muscle very quickly supplies phosphate for making new ATP during short maximum effort?
116056.e: Creatine phosphate passes its phosphate group directly to ADP. This store lasts a few seconds, for example during a sprint.
116056.m: Creatine phosphate is the fastest supply of ATP.

116057.q: Which enzyme in the inner mitochondrial membrane makes most of the ATP?
116057.e: ATP synthase uses the proton gradient of the respiratory chain like a turbine. Part of the enzyme rotates and joins ADP to phosphate.
116057.m: ATP synthase works like a molecular rotary motor.

116058.q: Which enzyme transfers the phosphate group from creatine phosphate to ADP?
116058.e: Creatine kinase catalyses the reaction creatine phosphate plus ADP to creatine plus ATP. The reaction is reversible.
116058.m: Creatine kinase makes ATP from creatine phosphate.

116059.q: How quickly can creatine phosphate rebuild used-up ATP in muscle?
116059.e: Creatine phosphate passes its phosphate group directly to ADP (Lohmann reaction). This means new ATP is available almost immediately.
116059.m: Creatine phosphate supplies new ATP in fractions of a second.

116060.q: Roughly how long does the creatine phosphate store last under maximum effort?
116060.e: Creatine phosphate supplies energy very quickly, but the store is small. After a few seconds glycolysis increasingly takes over.
116060.m: Creatine phosphate only lasts for a few seconds of top performance.

116061.q: In which sport is the creatine phosphate store the most important energy source?
116061.e: Short, maximum efforts are mainly covered by ATP and creatine phosphate. This store is nowhere near enough for long distances.
116061.m: For short sprints, muscle mainly uses creatine phosphate.

116062.q: What is energy supply via creatine phosphate called in sports physiology?
116062.e: In this process no oxygen is used and no lactate is formed. That is why it is called anaerobic and alactic.
116062.m: Splitting creatine phosphate works without oxygen and without lactate.

116063.q: Which breakdown product of creatine is excreted by the kidneys and serves as a measure of kidney function?
116063.e: Creatine and creatine phosphate are constantly converted into creatinine in small amounts. If the creatinine level in the blood rises, the kidneys are filtering less well.
116063.m: A high creatinine level in the blood points to weak kidney function.

116064.q: Where does the creatine in our muscles come from?
a: The body makes it itself and takes it in with meat and fish
It forms only from sugar in the muscles
It is taken in only with dairy products
Gut bacteria supply it as a vitamin
116064.e: The kidneys and liver make creatine from amino acids. We also take it in with meat and fish; vegetarians often have somewhat smaller stores.
116064.m: Creatine is made by the body and taken in with meat and fish.

116065.q: What does a greatly raised level of creatine kinase in the blood usually indicate?
116065.e: Creatine kinase sits in muscle cells and gets into the blood when they are damaged. It is raised, for example, after a heart attack, injuries or very hard exercise.
116065.m: Creatine kinase in the blood is a marker of muscle damage.

116066.q: Roughly how high is the lactate concentration in the blood of a healthy person at rest?
116066.e: At rest the blood lactate level is usually between about 0.5 and 2 mmol per litre. Under maximum effort it can rise to over 15 mmol per litre.
116066.m: Even at rest the blood contains some lactate.

116067.q: How does lactate formation benefit anaerobic glycolysis?
116067.e: When pyruvate is converted to lactate, NADH is oxidised to NAD+. Without NAD+, glycolysis would come to a standstill.

116068.q: What is the cycle called in which lactate from muscle is rebuilt into glucose in the liver?
116068.e: Lactate travels through the blood to the liver, where it becomes glucose by gluconeogenesis. This glucose can return to the muscle.
116068.m: In the Cori cycle the liver recycles lactate into glucose.

116069.q: What is now considered the main cause of muscle soreness after exercise?
a: Small injuries in the muscle fibres
116069.e: Lactate is usually broken down within one to two hours, but muscle soreness only appears later. It is put down to tiny tears and inflammation.
116069.m: Muscle soreness is caused by micro-injuries, not by lactate.

116070.q: Which blood lactate value was classically set as the aerobic-anaerobic threshold?
116070.e: Mader's 4 mmol threshold was used in training planning for a long time. Today the threshold is often determined individually.
116070.m: Classically, the anaerobic threshold is 4 mmol of lactate per litre.

116071.q: Which tissues use lactate from the blood as a source of energy?
a: The heart and slow muscle fibres
116071.e: Lactate is not a waste product but a fuel. Heart muscle and oxidative fibres convert it into pyruvate and burn it in the mitochondria.
116071.m: Lactate can be used as fuel by the heart and muscles.

116072.q: How can the breakdown of lactate after hard exercise be speeded up?
a: By jogging gently to cool down
116072.e: With light movement, blood flow stays high and the muscles burn lactate. Lying completely still slows the breakdown.
116072.m: Active recovery breaks down lactate faster.

116073.q: In which running distance does anaerobic glycolysis with lactate formation play a particularly large role?
116073.e: High-intensity effort lasting about 30 seconds to 2 minutes is largely covered by anaerobic glycolysis. That is why 400 m runners reach very high lactate levels.
116073.m: In the 400 m, lactate rises especially sharply.

116074.q: What does a muscle spindle measure?
a: The length and stretch of the muscle
The oxygen content in the muscle
116074.e: Muscle spindles are stretch receptors that lie parallel to the working fibres. They report the muscle's length and how it changes.
116074.m: Muscle spindles report the stretch of the muscle to the spinal cord.

116075.q: Where are the muscle spindles located?
a: In skeletal muscle between the muscle fibres
In the tendon at the bone
In the skin over the muscle
116075.e: Muscle spindles are small, elongated sense organs that lie parallel to the working fibres in the muscle. So they are stretched along with the muscle every time.
116075.m: Muscle spindles lie in the muscle between the fibres.

116076.q: What is the stretch reflex for in everyday life?
a: It helps keep your posture stable
116076.e: If you start to sway while standing, muscles are stretched. The muscle spindles report this and the reflex tightens the muscles immediately.
116076.m: Stretch reflexes help stabilise your posture.

116077.q: Why does a doctor test the knee-jerk reflex with a reflex hammer?
a: To check the nerves and spinal cord
To put the kneecap back in place
116077.e: For the reflex to work, the muscle spindle, nerve fibres, spinal cord and muscle must all function. A missing or exaggerated reflex points to a problem.
116077.m: Reflexes show whether nerves and spinal cord are working properly.

116078.q: Which reflex is based on muscle spindles being stimulated by a tap on the tendon below the kneecap?
116078.e: The tap briefly stretches the quadriceps and the spindles report this to the spinal cord. The alpha motor neuron makes the muscle twitch and the leg kicks forwards.
116078.m: The knee-jerk reflex is a classic stretch reflex.

116079.q: How many synapses lie in the central reflex arc of the muscle stretch reflex?
116079.e: The Ia fibre ends directly on the alpha motor neuron in the spinal cord. This monosynaptic reflex is therefore especially fast.

116080.q: Unlike the muscle spindle, which receptor mainly measures the tension in the muscle?
116080.e: The Golgi tendon organ lies at the junction of muscle and tendon, in series with the muscle fibres. It reports the pulling tension via Ib fibres.
116080.m: The Golgi tendon organ measures muscle tension.

116081.q: What are sensory receptors such as the muscle spindle called that give information about the position and movement of your own body?
116081.e: Proprioceptors in muscles, tendons and joints report length, tension and position. Nociceptors report pain, photoreceptors light.

116082.q: Thanks to the muscle spindles, what can you sense even with your eyes closed?
a: The position of your own arms and legs
116082.e: The muscle spindles constantly report how much each muscle is stretched. From this the brain works out where the arms and legs are at that moment.
116082.m: Muscle spindles tell the brain the position of the limbs.

116083.q: Which property fits type I muscle fibres?
116083.e: Type I fibres contract slowly, work oxidatively and hardly tire. They are also called slow-twitch fibres.
116083.m: Type I fibres are slow endurance fibres.

116084.q: Which muscle fibres do sprinters mainly use for short, explosive efforts?
116084.e: Type II fibres contract very quickly and powerfully but tire fast. Sprinters have especially many of them in their legs.
116084.m: Fast type II fibres provide explosive power.

116085.q: Which pigment gives type I fibres their red colour?
116085.e: Myoglobin stores oxygen in the muscle and is red. Endurance fibres contain a particularly large amount of it.
116085.m: Myoglobin makes the slow fibres red.

116086.q: Which athletes usually have an especially high proportion of type I fibres in their leg muscles?
116086.e: Endurance athletes often have well over half type I fibres. Sprinters, by contrast, have many fast type II fibres.
116086.m: Endurance athletes have many slow fibres.

116087.q: Why are fast type II fibres often called “white” muscle fibres?
116087.e: The red pigment myoglobin stores oxygen. Fast fibres work more without oxygen and contain less of it, so they look paler.
116087.m: Fast fibres are paler because they contain little myoglobin.

116088.q: How do fast type II fibres mainly get their energy during short maximum efforts?
a: By breaking down glucose without oxygen
116088.e: Anaerobic glycolysis produces ATP quickly, but only a little and with lactate as a by-product. That is why these fibres tire quickly.
116088.m: Fast fibres mainly get energy without oxygen.

116089.q: Which muscle fibres does the body mainly use during light, long activity such as walking?
116089.e: At low force, the small motor units with slow, enduring fibres are activated first. Fast fibres only join in at high force.
116089.m: During light activity, mainly the slow fibres work.

116090.q: Why are type I fibres surrounded by especially many capillaries?
a: They need a lot of oxygen
116090.e: Type I fibres make their ATP aerobically and need a good oxygen supply for this. A high density of capillaries shortens the diffusion distances.
116090.m: Endurance fibres are densely supplied with capillaries.

a: The muscle length stays the same
The muscle tension stays the same
116091.e: In an isometric contraction the tension rises without the muscle shortening. Isometric means equal measure.
116091.m: In an isometric contraction the length does not change.

116092.q: What is a contraction called in which the muscle shortens while the tension stays the same?
116092.e: Isotonic means equal tension. The muscle shortens and moves a constant load.
116092.m: In an isotonic contraction the tension stays constant.

116093.q: What is a contraction called in which the length and tension of the muscle change at the same time?
116093.e: Most everyday movements are auxotonic. Force and muscle length change at the same time.
116093.m: Auxotonic contraction is the most common in everyday life.

116094.q: Which exercise is a typical example of mainly isometric muscle work?
116094.e: In the forearm plank the trunk muscles hold the body still in position. The muscles are tense but hardly change their length.
116094.m: Holding exercises train the muscle isometrically.

116095.q: How much physical work does a person do on a dumbbell while holding it still?
116095.e: Work is force times distance in the direction of the force. Without movement the distance is zero, even though the muscle uses energy and gets tired.
116095.m: Without distance, no mechanical work is done on the load.

116096.q: What is a contraction called in which the muscle is lengthened under tension, for example when walking downhill?
116096.e: When walking downhill, the thigh muscle brakes the movement while it is being stretched. Concentric, on the other hand, would mean that it shortens.
116096.m: Eccentric work is the muscle's braking work.

116097.q: In which type of contraction can a muscle develop the greatest force?
116097.e: In eccentric work, cross-bridges that are already bound are stretched further and can withstand more. That is why the force is greater than in isometric or concentric work.
116097.m: A muscle is strongest when working eccentrically.

116098.q: Why is blood flow restricted during strong isometric tension?
a: The muscle squeezes its own blood vessels
116098.e: A strongly tensed muscle raises the pressure in the tissue and compresses the vessels. That is why it tires relatively quickly during holding work.
116098.m: Strong holding work reduces blood flow to the muscle.

116099.q: What is the main task of the sarcoplasmic reticulum in the muscle fibre?
116099.e: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a specialised endoplasmic reticulum. It releases calcium for contraction and takes it back up afterwards.
116099.m: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is the muscle's calcium store.

116100.q: What happens in the muscle when calcium is pumped back into the store after a contraction?
a: The muscle no longer uses any ATP
116100.e: Without calcium in the cytosol, the myosin heads can no longer bind to actin. The filaments slide back and the muscle relaxes.
116100.m: Without free calcium the muscle relaxes.

116101.q: What triggers the release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum?
a: An action potential on the muscle fibre
116101.e: A nerve impulse excites the muscle fibre. The action potential travels into the fibre and opens the calcium store there.
116101.m: Excitation opens the muscle's calcium store.

116102.q: What are the T tubules of a muscle fibre for?
a: They carry the excitation into the inside of the fibre
They transport blood into the fibre
116102.e: T tubules are infoldings of the cell membrane. Through them the action potential quickly reaches the sarcoplasmic reticulum deep in the fibre.
116102.m: T tubules carry the excitation into the fibre.

116103.q: Why does a body become stiff a few hours after death?
a: Without ATP the myosin heads no longer detach from the actin
The blood freezes in the muscles
The bones grow together with the muscles
116103.e: After death, calcium leaks out of the store and myosin binds to actin. The ATP needed to release this bond is missing, so the muscles stay stiff.
116103.m: Without ATP, actin and myosin stay connected.

116104.q: Which organelle of other cells is the sarcoplasmic reticulum related to?
116104.e: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a specialised endoplasmic reticulum. In muscle it serves mainly as a calcium store.
116104.m: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is the ER of the muscle cell.

116105.q: What happens if too much calcium is constantly released in a muscle fibre?
a: The muscle becomes insensitive to nerves
116105.e: Calcium starts the contraction. If it stays in the cytosol, the myosin heads keep binding to actin and the muscle cramps.
116105.m: Too much calcium in the cytosol leads to muscle cramps.

116106.q: What is the process called in which an action potential at the muscle membrane is turned into a contraction?
116106.e: The action potential travels through the T tubules into the fibre and leads to calcium release. Calcium then starts the cross-bridge cycle.
116106.m: Excitation-contraction coupling links excitation and contraction.

116107.q: How does the calcium concentration in the cytosol change when the muscle fibre is excited?
116107.e: At rest the cytosol contains very little calcium. On excitation, calcium flows out of the store and the concentration rises about a hundredfold.
116107.m: On excitation, calcium in the muscle rises sharply.

116108.q: A hammer head sits loosely on the handle. Why can you tighten it by banging the end of the handle hard on the floor?
a: The head keeps moving because of its inertia
The floor pushes the head downwards
The air presses the head onto the handle
116108.e: The handle is stopped abruptly by the floor, but the head keeps its speed. So it slides a little further onto the handle.
116108.m: A body keeps its state of motion as long as no force changes it.

116109.q: A stone circles on a string at a constant speed. Is there a resultant force acting on it?
a: Yes, because the direction changes all the time
No, because the speed stays constant
116109.e: Velocity is a vector, and its direction keeps changing on a circular path. According to the principle of inertia, this requires a resultant force.
116109.m: A change of direction also requires a resultant force.

116110.q: A book lies on a table. According to Newton’s third law, which force is the counterforce to the weight with which the Earth pulls the book?
a: The pull of the book on the Earth
The normal force of the table on the book
Static friction between book and table
The buoyancy of the book in air
116110.e: Force and counterforce always act between the same two bodies. The Earth pulls the book, so the book pulls on the Earth just as strongly.
116110.m: Force and counterforce always involve the same two bodies.

116111.q: A swimmer pushes off from the side of the pool with her feet. Which force accelerates her?
a: The force of the wall on her feet
The force of her feet on the wall
116111.e: The swimmer pushes against the wall, and according to the third law the wall pushes back just as strongly. Only this force acts on the swimmer and accelerates her.
116111.m: When you push off, you are accelerated by the counterforce.

116112.q: Which theory replaces Newtonian mechanics in describing electrons in the atomic shell?
116112.e: For very small particles, the classical idea of paths fails. Electrons in the atom are therefore described using quantum mechanics.
116112.m: In the atom, quantum mechanics applies instead of classical mechanics.

116113.q: A horse starts pulling a cart. Why does the horse start moving even though the cart pulls back just as strongly?
a: The ground pushes the horse forwards more strongly
The horse is heavier than the cart
The cart actually pulls more weakly
116113.e: For the horse’s motion, only the forces on the horse count. The friction force of the ground on the hooves is greater than the backward pull of the cart.
116113.m: Whether a body accelerates depends only on the forces acting on it.

116114.q: In which type of frame of reference do Newton’s laws apply without extra forces?
a: Only in the Sun’s centre-of-mass frame
116114.e: An inertial frame is a frame of reference in which the principle of inertia applies. In accelerated frames you also need fictitious forces.
116114.m: Newton’s laws apply in their simple form in inertial frames.

116115.q: A parachutist is descending at a constant speed. What is the resultant force on her?
a: Equal to the air resistance alone
116115.e: At constant speed, the acceleration is zero. Air resistance and weight are equal and opposite.
116115.m: At constant speed, the forces are balanced.

116116.q: Two people pull on the ends of a rope with 200 N each in opposite directions. What is the tension in the rope?
116116.e: Each person pulls with 200 N, and the rope transmits exactly this force. It is the same as if one end were fixed to a wall and the other pulled with 200 N.
116116.m: The tension equals the force at one end, not the sum of both ends.

116117.q: A resultant force of 12 N accelerates a body at 3 m/s². What is its mass?
116117.e: From the basic equation, m equals F divided by a. 12 N divided by 3 m/s² gives 4 kg.
116117.m: Inertial mass can be determined from force and acceleration.

116118.q: A force of 50 N acts without friction on a body with a mass of 25 kg. What is its acceleration?
116118.e: The acceleration is a equals F divided by m. 50 N divided by 25 kg gives 2 m/s².
116118.m: The greater the mass, the smaller the acceleration for the same force.

116119.q: In its most general form, Newton formulated force as the rate of change of which quantity?
116119.e: In general form, force is the time derivative of momentum. With constant mass, this gives mass times acceleration.
116119.m: Force is the rate of change of momentum.

116120.q: A car with a mass of 1000 kg accelerates steadily from 0 to 20 m/s in 8 s. What is the accelerating force?
116120.e: The acceleration is 20 m/s divided by 8 s, which is 2.5 m/s². Times 1000 kg, this gives 2500 N.
116120.m: The acceleration follows from the change in speed per unit of time.

116121.q: A force of 30 N pulls a 2 kg block without friction, which tows a second 4 kg block behind it on a rope. What is the force in the connecting rope?
116121.e: Both blocks together experience a equals 30 N divided by 6 kg, which is 5 m/s². The rope has to accelerate the 4 kg block, so 4 kg times 5 m/s² equals 20 N.
116121.m: A rope transmits exactly the force the towed body needs for its acceleration.

116122.q: A 0.5 kg ball is falling, and the air resistance at this moment is 1 N. What is its acceleration (g equals 9.81 m/s²)?
116122.e: The weight is 4.905 N; minus 1 N leaves 3.905 N. Divided by 0.5 kg, this gives 7.81 m/s².
116122.m: Only the resultant force counts for the acceleration.

116123.q: A body slides without friction down a slope inclined at 30°. Roughly what is its acceleration (g equals 9.81 m/s²)?
116123.e: The force down the slope is m times g times sin 30°. Because sin 30° equals 0.5, the acceleration is about 4.9 m/s².
116123.m: On a slope, only the component down the slope accelerates the body.

116124.q: How does a body’s acceleration change if you double the force and at the same time double the mass?
116124.e: Acceleration is the quotient of force and mass. If numerator and denominator are both doubled, the quotient stays unchanged.
116124.m: Acceleration depends on the ratio of force to mass.

116125.q: What is the SI unit of momentum expressed in base units?
116125.e: Momentum is mass times velocity. This gives the unit kilograms times metres per second.
116125.m: Momentum is given in kilograms times metres per second.

116126.q: What kind of physical quantity is momentum?
116126.e: Momentum has magnitude and direction. That is why momenta in collisions must be added as vectors.
116126.m: Momentum has a direction and is a vector.

116127.q: What is the momentum of a ball with a mass of 0.16 kg and a speed of 25 m/s?
116127.e: The momentum is 0.16 kg times 25 m/s. That gives 4 kg·m/s.
116127.m: For momentum, multiply mass and velocity.

116128.q: A 10 t lorry is travelling at 1 m/s, a 1 t car at 10 m/s. What is true of the size of their momenta?
a: The lorry has ten times the momentum
The car has ten times the momentum
The car has a hundred times the momentum
116128.e: Both have 10,000 kg·m/s, because 10,000 kg times 1 m/s equals 1000 kg times 10 m/s. Their kinetic energies, however, are different.
116128.m: A small mass at high speed can have the same momentum as a large mass at low speed.

116129.q: Two bodies have the same size of momentum but different masses. Which has the greater kinetic energy?
116129.e: Kinetic energy can be written as momentum squared divided by twice the mass. For the same momentum, it is therefore greater for the smaller mass.
116129.m: For the same momentum, the lighter body has more kinetic energy.

116130.q: A 0.3 kg ball hits a wall head-on at 10 m/s and bounces back at 10 m/s. What is the size of its change in momentum?
116130.e: The momentum changes from plus 3 kg·m/s to minus 3 kg·m/s. The difference is therefore 6 kg·m/s.
116130.m: When bouncing back, momentum reverses direction, so the change is twice as large.

116131.q: What is true of the momentum of a body moving at almost the speed of light?
a: It is greater than mass times velocity
It is exactly mass times velocity
It is smaller than mass times velocity
116131.e: Relativistically, momentum is also multiplied by the Lorentz factor, which is greater than 1. Close to the speed of light, momentum grows without limit.
116131.m: At very high speeds, momentum must be calculated relativistically.

a: Yes, even though photons have no mass
No, because photons have no mass
Only in glass, not in a vacuum
116132.e: A photon has a momentum of Planck’s constant divided by wavelength. Radiation pressure and the idea of solar sails are based on this.

116133.q: Under what condition is the total momentum of a system conserved?
a: Only when all collisions are elastic
Only when all bodies are at rest
Only when internal friction is zero
116133.e: In an isolated system, all internal forces cancel each other out in pairs. That is why total momentum can only change through external forces.
116133.m: In an isolated system, total momentum stays constant.

116134.q: Why does a small rowing boat move backwards when you jump forwards from it onto land?
a: Because the wind pushes against it
116134.e: Before the jump, person and boat are at rest, so total momentum is zero. If the person gains momentum forwards when jumping, the boat gains the same amount of momentum backwards.
116134.m: If you jump forwards from a boat, the boat moves backwards.

116135.q: A body at rest breaks into two parts due to an internal explosion. What is the total momentum of the fragments afterwards?
a: Equal to the momentum of the heavier part
116135.e: Beforehand total momentum was zero, and the explosion is an internal force. The parts therefore fly apart with equal and opposite momenta.
116135.m: Internal forces do not change total momentum.

116136.q: A 1 kg trolley travels at 4 m/s into a stationary 3 kg trolley. After the collision, the first trolley is at rest. How fast does the second trolley move afterwards?
116136.e: The momentum before is 1 kg times 4 m/s, which is 4 kg·m/s. The second trolley takes all of it, so 4 divided by 3 equals about 1.3 m/s.
116136.m: All the momentum before the collision is in the moving bodies afterwards.

116137.q: Does the law of conservation of momentum also apply to inelastic collisions?
a: Yes, always in an isolated system
Only if the bodies have the same mass
Only if the bodies are at rest afterwards
116137.e: In inelastic collisions, some of the kinetic energy is converted into other forms of energy. Momentum, however, is still fully conserved.
116137.m: Momentum is conserved in every kind of collision.

116138.q: How do you apply the law of conservation of momentum to an oblique collision in a plane?
a: Only for the sizes of the momenta
Only along the original direction of motion
Not at all, it only applies to head-on collisions
116138.e: Momentum is a vector, so each of its components is conserved separately. In snooker, this applies in the x and y directions.
116138.m: In oblique collisions, each component of momentum is conserved.

116139.q: Which particle did Wolfgang Pauli propose in 1930, partly to save the conservation of energy and momentum in beta decay?
116139.e: In beta decay, energy and momentum seemed to be missing. Pauli suggested a neutral, hardly detectable particle, which was only discovered in 1956.
116139.m: The neutrino was proposed so that the conservation laws also hold in beta decay.

116140.q: A 2 kg trolley moves to the right at 3 m/s, a 1 kg trolley to the left at 2 m/s. What is the total momentum of the system?
116140.e: Momenta are added with signs. 2 kg times 3 m/s minus 1 kg times 2 m/s gives 4 kg·m/s to the right.
116140.m: When adding momenta, you have to take direction into account.

116141.q: Which quantities are conserved in a perfectly elastic collision?
116141.e: In an elastic collision, no kinetic energy is converted into other forms of energy. So besides momentum, kinetic energy is also conserved.
116141.m: In an elastic collision, kinetic energy is also conserved.

116142.q: A snooker ball hits an identical stationary ball head-on and elastically. What happens?
a: The first ball stops and the second takes over its speed
Both roll on at half speed
Both bounce off in opposite directions
The first rolls back at double speed
116142.e: With equal masses, the balls swap their velocities in a head-on elastic collision. This is also how Newton’s cradle works.
116142.m: Bodies of equal mass swap velocities in an elastic collision.

116143.q: A 2 kg body hits a stationary 1 kg body head-on and elastically at 3 m/s. How fast is the lighter body afterwards?
116143.e: For the body that is hit, v equals 2 times m1 divided by the sum of the masses times 3 m/s. That is 4 divided by 3 times 3 m/s, which equals 4 m/s.
116143.m: In an elastic collision, the lighter partner can become faster than the body that hits it.

116144.q: A very heavy body hits a very light stationary body head-on and elastically. Roughly how fast does the light body become?
a: About twice as fast as the heavy one
About as fast as the heavy one
About half as fast as the heavy one
116144.e: In the limiting case of very unequal masses, the heavy body moves on almost unchanged. The light body gains about double the speed.
116144.m: A heavy collision partner flings a light one away at almost double speed.

116145.q: What is the coefficient of restitution, the ratio of separation speed to approach speed, in a perfectly elastic collision?
116145.e: In a perfectly elastic collision, the bodies move apart with the same relative speed at which they approached. The ratio is therefore 1.
116145.m: The coefficient of restitution of a perfectly elastic collision is one.

116146.q: A ball bounces perfectly elastically head-on off a very heavy stationary wall. What is its velocity afterwards?
a: The same size, but in the opposite direction
116146.e: Because of its huge mass, the wall takes up practically no energy. The ball keeps its speed and flies back.
116146.m: At an elastic obstacle, only the direction is reversed.

116147.q: Why are substances containing hydrogen, such as water, particularly good at slowing down fast neutrons in nuclear reactors?
a: Hydrogen nuclei are almost as heavy as neutrons
Hydrogen is electrically charged like neutrons
116147.e: In an elastic collision, the most energy is transferred when both masses are about the same. A proton has almost the mass of a neutron.
116147.m: Collision partners of equal mass slow each other down most effectively.

116148.q: At what angle do two balls of equal mass move apart after an oblique elastic collision if one was at rest beforehand?
116148.e: For equal masses, conservation of momentum and energy give a right angle between the paths. You can see this in snooker with off-centre shots.
116148.m: Balls of equal mass move apart at right angles after an oblique elastic collision.

116149.q: What characterises a perfectly inelastic collision?
a: The bodies move on together afterwards
The bodies bounce off at the same speed
116149.e: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the bodies stick together and afterwards have the same velocity. Some of the kinetic energy is converted.
116149.m: After a perfectly inelastic collision, both bodies have the same velocity.

116150.q: A 1500 kg car travelling at 20 m/s runs into a stationary 500 kg car, and the two get wedged together. How fast do they move immediately afterwards?
116150.e: The momentum before is 30,000 kg·m/s. Shared over 2000 kg, this gives a common velocity of 15 m/s.
116150.m: In an inelastic collision, total momentum is shared over the combined mass.

116151.q: A body hits a stationary body of equal mass in a perfectly inelastic collision. What share of the kinetic energy is lost?
116151.e: The common velocity is half as large, and double the mass moves on. The kinetic energy afterwards is only half.
116151.m: In an inelastic collision of equal masses, half the kinetic energy remains.

116152.q: A 2 kg body at 6 m/s hits a stationary 4 kg body in a perfectly inelastic collision. How much kinetic energy is converted?
116152.e: Before, it is 0.5 times 2 kg times 36 m²/s², which equals 36 J. The common velocity is 2 m/s, so afterwards 12 J; the loss is 24 J.
116152.m: In an inelastic collision, some of the kinetic energy is converted into other forms of energy.

116153.q: What is a ballistic pendulum used for?
a: To measure the speed of projectiles
116153.e: The projectile gets stuck in the pendulum body, which then swings out. The projectile’s speed can be calculated from the height reached and the conservation of momentum.
116153.m: The ballistic pendulum makes high projectile speeds measurable.

116154.q: A 10 g bullet gets stuck in a stationary 990 g block of wood. Both then move at 2 m/s. How fast was the bullet?
116154.e: After the collision, the momentum is 1 kg times 2 m/s, which is 2 kg·m/s. This came from the bullet, so 2 divided by 0.01 kg equals 200 m/s.
116154.m: From the shared momentum after the collision, you get the speed of the bullet.

116155.q: Where does the kinetic energy go that is lost in an inelastic collision?
a: Into the mass of the bodies
116155.e: Energy is never lost, only converted. In a car crash, the crumple zone deforms and heats up.
116155.m: In an inelastic collision, kinetic energy is converted into work of deformation and heat.

116156.q: Two balls of modelling clay of equal mass fly towards each other at the same speed and stick together. What share of the kinetic energy is kept?
116156.e: Total momentum beforehand is zero, so the lump is at rest afterwards. All the kinetic energy has been converted into other forms of energy.
116156.m: With equal and opposite momenta, a sticking lump comes to a standstill.

116157.q: A ball falls from a height of 1 m onto the floor and then bounces up 0.64 m. What is the coefficient of restitution of this partly elastic collision?
116157.e: The coefficient of restitution is the ratio of the speeds after and before impact. Because speed grows with the square root of height, the square root of 0.64 gives 0.8.
116157.m: The coefficient of restitution can be calculated from drop and bounce height using a square root.

116158.q: Which conservation law is the recoil principle based on?
116158.e: If mass is expelled in one direction, the rest gains an equal momentum in the opposite direction. Total momentum stays unchanged.
116158.m: Recoil is a direct consequence of the conservation of momentum.

116159.q: A 4 kg rifle fires a 10 g bullet at 800 m/s. At what speed does the rifle recoil?
116159.e: The bullet’s momentum is 0.01 kg times 800 m/s, which is 8 kg·m/s. The rifle gains the same momentum, so 8 divided by 4 equals 2 m/s.
116159.m: The heavy rifle recoils much more slowly than the light bullet flies.

116160.q: Two ice skaters of 60 kg and 40 kg stand still and push off from each other. The heavier one glides away at 2 m/s. How fast is the lighter one?
116160.e: The two momenta must add up to zero. 60 kg times 2 m/s equals 120 kg·m/s, and divided by 40 kg this gives 3 m/s.
116160.m: After pushing off, both partners have equal and opposite momenta.

116161.q: How do squid move when fleeing quickly?
a: By expelling water using the recoil principle
By beating their pectoral fins quickly
By pushing off from the sea floor
116161.e: Squid suck water into their mantle and squeeze it out through a funnel. The recoil drives them in the opposite direction.
116161.m: Squid use recoil like a jet engine.

116162.q: Why do firefighters have to hold a nozzle with a high water flow firmly?
a: The jet of water coming out produces a recoil
The water in the hose is very hot
The hose contracts because of the cold
The air presses on the nozzle
116162.e: The water is accelerated forwards at high speed. According to the conservation of momentum, an equal force acts backwards on the nozzle.
116162.m: A fast jet of water pushes the nozzle backwards.

116163.q: Why does a lawn sprinkler with curved nozzle arms turn by itself?
a: The water coming out produces a recoil
A small motor inside drives it
The water pulls the arms forwards
116163.e: The water is expelled backwards from the curved arms. According to the conservation of momentum, a force acts on the arms in the opposite direction, and the sprinkler turns.
116163.m: A lawn sprinkler turns because of recoil.

116164.q: A 100 kg astronaut is floating at rest in space and throws a 2 kg tool away at 5 m/s. How fast does she move afterwards?
116164.e: The tool gains 2 kg times 5 m/s, which is 10 kg·m/s. The astronaut gains the same momentum in the opposite direction, so 10 divided by 100 equals 0.1 m/s.
116164.m: If you throw something away in space, you move in the opposite direction.

116165.q: How does an aircraft’s jet engine produce its thrust?
a: It expels gas backwards at high speed
It sucks the aircraft forwards with low pressure
It pushes air against the wings
116165.e: The engine strongly accelerates air and combustion gases backwards. The change in momentum of the gas stream gives a thrust force forwards.
116165.m: A jet engine works by the recoil principle.

116166.q: Which scientist published the rocket equation named after him in 1903?
116166.e: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky is regarded as a pioneer of space flight theory. The rocket equation is therefore also called the Tsiolkovsky equation.
116166.m: The rocket equation goes back to Konstantin Tsiolkovsky.

116167.q: According to the rocket equation, which two quantities does the achievable change in velocity of a rocket without external forces depend on?
a: Burn time and launch mass alone
Type of fuel and air pressure
116167.e: The change in velocity is the exhaust velocity times the natural logarithm of the ratio of launch mass to final mass. The burn time plays no part.
116167.m: A rocket’s final velocity depends on the mass ratio and the exhaust velocity.

116168.q: A rocket has an exhaust velocity of 3000 m/s and a mass ratio of 4. Roughly what change in velocity does it reach without external forces?
116168.e: This is 3000 m/s times ln 4. Because ln 4 is about 1.386, the result is about 4160 m/s.
116168.m: The final velocity only grows with the logarithm of the mass ratio.

116169.q: Roughly what mass ratio does a rocket need to reach a change in velocity of twice its exhaust velocity?
116169.e: From ln of m0 divided by m1 equals 2, it follows that m0 divided by m1 equals e to the power of 2. That is about 7.39.
116169.m: For each additional exhaust velocity of final speed, the required mass ratio grows by a factor of e.

116170.q: From what mass ratio does a rocket become faster than its own exhaust velocity?
116170.e: The change in velocity exceeds the exhaust velocity as soon as the logarithm is greater than 1. This is the case from Euler’s number e upwards.
116170.m: A rocket can become faster than its exhaust jet.

116171.q: Why are rockets for reaching orbit usually built with several stages?
a: Empty tanks are dropped, improving the mass ratio
Each stage has an exhaust velocity higher than light
Several stages reduce air resistance to zero
The Earth’s gravity only acts on the first stage
116171.e: Empty tanks and engines would otherwise be dead weight that would have to be accelerated further. By dropping them, each stage achieves a better mass ratio.

116172.q: A rocket expels 100 kg of gas per second at 2500 m/s. What is its thrust?
116172.e: Thrust is the mass flow times the exhaust velocity. 100 kg/s times 2500 m/s gives 250,000 N.
116172.m: Thrust is the product of mass expelled per second and exhaust velocity.

116173.q: Which mathematical function links the mass ratio with the change in velocity in the rocket equation?
116173.e: Because the rocket keeps getting lighter while it burns, you have to integrate over the mass. This gives the natural logarithm.
116173.m: The rocket equation contains a natural logarithm.

116208.q: Why can plants hardly take up any water from very dry soil?
a: The remaining water clings tightly to the soil particles
Dry soil contains no water at all
The roots go to sleep in drought
116208.e: The drier the soil, the more tightly the remaining water is bound to soil particles. The root can then no longer draw it in, and the plant wilts.
116208.m: In dry soil, the water is tightly bound.

116209.q: By definition, what is the water potential of pure water at normal pressure and the same height?
116209.e: Pure, free water under standard conditions is the reference point and has a water potential of zero.
116209.m: Pure water has a water potential of zero; solutions have negative values.

116210.q: In which direction does water move by itself in a plant?
a: From higher to lower water potential
From lower to higher water potential
Always from the phloem into the xylem
116210.e: Water flows passively to where its water potential is lower, that is, more negative. This is how it travels from the soil through the root into the atmosphere.
116210.m: Water always flows towards the more negative water potential.

116211.q: Why do plants wilt if you water them with very salty water?
a: The water potential of the soil falls below that of the root
Salt immediately blocks all the stomata
Salt destroys the chlorophyll within minutes
116211.e: Dissolved salt makes the water potential of the soil water very negative. If it is lower than in the root, the plant can no longer take up water or even loses some.
116211.m: Salty soil takes water away from the root instead of supplying it.

116212.q: Which process mainly pulls water up a tall tree?
116212.e: When water evaporates from the leaves, it creates suction. Because water molecules stick together, an unbroken column of water is pulled from the root up to the crown.
116212.m: The pull of evaporation draws water up the tree.

116213.q: What is the water potential of a cell with an osmotic potential of -0.8 MPa and a pressure potential of 0.5 MPa?
116213.e: The water potential is the sum of its components. -0.8 MPa + 0.5 MPa = -0.3 MPa.
116213.m: Water potential is the sum of osmotic potential and pressure potential.

116214.q: What happens to a plant cell that is placed in pure water?
a: It takes up water and becomes firm
116214.e: Many substances are dissolved in the cell sap, so water flows into the cell by osmosis. The rigid cell wall stops it from bursting, and the cell becomes firm.
116214.m: In pure water, a plant cell takes up water by osmosis.

116215.q: In which weather do plants lose the most water through evaporation?
116215.e: Dry, warm air takes up a lot of water vapour, and wind carries the damp air away from the leaf. That is when water loss is greatest.
116215.m: Warmth, dry air and wind increase evaporation.

116216.q: Why do trees not grow upwards without limit?
a: Water can only be pulled up to a certain height
The air gets too warm at the top
116216.e: The taller the tree, the stronger the suction must be to pull water up against gravity. Above 100 metres the water column breaks easily, which is why there are hardly any taller trees.
116216.m: Water transport limits the height of trees.

116217.q: According to the cohesion theory, what pulls water up a tree?
a: The suction caused by evaporation from the leaves
116217.e: Henry Dixon and John Joly explained in 1894 that when water evaporates from the leaves, it pulls the continuous column of water in the xylem after it. The cohesion of the water molecules stops it from breaking.
116217.m: Evaporation from the leaves pulls water up the tree.

116218.q: Which bonds are responsible for the cohesion between water molecules?
116218.e: Water molecules are dipoles and attract each other through hydrogen bonds. This cohesion keeps the water column in the xylem from breaking.
116218.m: Hydrogen bonds hold water molecules together as a column.

116219.q: What is the sticking of water molecules to the walls of the transport vessels called?
116219.e: Adhesion is the attraction between different substances, here between water and the cell wall. It helps to stabilise the water column.
116219.m: Adhesion binds water to other surfaces such as the vessel wall.

116220.q: Under what pressure is the water column in the xylem of a transpiring plant?
116220.e: The water column is pulled from above and is therefore under negative pressure. If you pierced a vessel, air would be sucked in rather than water pushed out.
116220.m: In the xylem, water is pulled, not pushed.

116221.q: What is the breaking of the water column in the xylem, in which gas bubbles form, called?
116221.e: Under very strong tension the water column can break and a gas bubble forms (embolism). The affected vessel element then stops working for transport.
116221.m: Cavitation breaks the water column with a gas bubble.

116222.q: Why can air pressure alone not lift water into the crown of a 30-metre-tall tree?
a: It can only support a column of water about 10 metres high
It only acts on the plant at night
It is cancelled out in the roots
116222.e: Air pressure of about 1 bar corresponds to a column of water about 10 metres high. Taller trees need the pull from above through cohesion.
116222.m: Air pressure can only lift water about 10 metres.

116223.q: Which tree species does the tallest known living tree on Earth belong to?
116223.e: The coast redwood “Hyperion” in California is almost 116 metres tall. Even to that height, water is pulled up by cohesion. The tallest eucalyptus reaches about 100 metres.
116223.m: The tallest known tree is a coast redwood in California.

116224.q: In which tissue does the continuous column of water rise from the root to the leaf?
116224.e: The xylem (woody part) carries water and minerals upwards. The phloem, on the other hand, mainly transports sugar.
116224.m: Water rises in the xylem from the root to the leaves.

116225.q: Why can capillarity alone not lift water into the crown of a tall tree?
a: In such fine tubes it only lifts water a few metres
It only works in glass tubes
116225.e: In vessels a few micrometres in radius, water rises by capillarity only about one to two metres. Tall trees need the pull of evaporation and cohesion.
116225.m: Capillarity only lifts water a few metres in plant vessels.

116226.q: Where does the transpiration pull mainly start?
a: At the cell walls of the mesophyll in the leaf
In the cambium of the trunk
In the sieve tubes of the bark
116226.e: Water evaporates from the moist cell walls of the mesophyll into the air spaces and escapes through the stomata. This draws more water up from the xylem.
116226.m: The pull begins where water evaporates in the leaf.

116227.q: What proportion of the water taken up by the root does a plant typically transpire again?
116227.e: Only a small part of the water is used for photosynthesis and growth. By far the largest part, usually over 90 per cent, evaporates through the leaves.
116227.m: Almost all the water taken up evaporates again through the leaves.

116228.q: In which weather conditions is transpiration strongest?
116228.e: Warmth and dry air increase the water potential gradient to the air, and light opens the stomata. Wind carries away the layer of damp air on the leaf.
116228.m: Warm, dry, moving air drives transpiration.

116229.q: By which route does most of the transpired water leave a leaf?
116229.e: The leaf surface is almost watertight thanks to a waxy layer. Most of the water escapes as stomatal transpiration.
116229.m: Most transpiration happens through the stomata.

116230.q: Which device measures the water uptake of a cut shoot as a measure of transpiration?
116230.e: In a potometer, the shoot is placed in a tube filled with water. The movement of an air bubble shows how much water is taken up.
116230.m: A potometer measures how much water a shoot takes up.

116231.q: Why does wind increase the transpiration of a leaf?
a: It removes the damp boundary layer above the leaf
116231.e: A thin layer of damp, still air forms above the leaf. Wind carries it away, so the gradient to the dry air stays large.
116231.m: Wind thins the damp layer of air and so speeds up evaporation.

116232.q: How does transpiration benefit the temperature of the leaf?
a: It warms the leaf at night
It stores heat in the xylem
116232.e: Water needs a lot of energy to evaporate, and this energy is taken from the leaf. So leaves overheat less in the sun.
116232.m: Transpiration cools leaves just as sweating cools the body.

116233.q: Why does the root take up water from moist soil when the plant is transpiring?
a: The water potential in the root is lower than in the soil
The soil actively presses the water in
The root uses ATP for every water molecule
116233.e: The pull from the leaves lowers the water potential in the xylem all the way down to the root. Water passively follows the gradient from the soil into the root.
116233.m: The root takes up water passively along the water potential gradient.

a: Giving off liquid water as droplets
Giving off water vapour through the stomata
Taking up dew through the leaves
Releasing sugar into the sieve tube
116234.e: In guttation, the plant presses out water in liquid form through special openings. Droplets form at the tips and edges of the leaves.
116234.m: In guttation, the plant gives off droplets of water.

116235.q: Through which structures is water given off during guttation?
