116858.e: The stent sits folded up on a balloon catheter. When the balloon is filled under pressure, the stent expands and presses against the vessel wall.
116858.m: A balloon presses the stent against the vessel wall.

116859.q: Who is the term “stent” named after?
116859.e: The name goes back to the English dentist Charles Stent, who developed an impression material in the 19th century. His name was later used for support materials.
116859.m: The stent owes its name to an English dentist.

116860.q: What is done in a heart bypass operation?
a: A narrowing is bypassed with a replacement vessel
116860.e: A vessel is connected so that the blood flows around the narrowed part of the coronary artery. Bypass means a way around.
116860.m: A bypass leads the blood past a narrowing.

116861.q: Which disease most often makes a heart bypass operation necessary?
a: Coronary arteries narrowed by hardening of the arteries
A heartbeat that is too slow
A hole in the septum of the heart
116861.e: In coronary heart disease, deposits build up in the coronary arteries. The heart muscle gets too little blood, and a bypass leads the blood past the narrowing.
116861.m: A bypass helps with narrowed coronary arteries.

116862.q: From which part of the body is a piece of vein often taken for a vein bypass on the heart?
116862.e: The superficial great saphenous vein in the leg is long, easy to reach and can be spared. A piece of it is inserted between the aorta and the coronary artery.
116862.m: Vein bypasses often use a vein from the leg.

116863.q: Which machine temporarily takes over the work of the heart and lungs in many bypass operations?
116863.e: The heart-lung machine pumps the blood and enriches it with oxygen. This allows surgeons to operate on the stopped heart.
116863.m: The heart-lung machine replaces the heart and lungs during the operation.

116864.q: How is the chest usually opened for a classic bypass operation?
116864.e: In a median sternotomy, the breastbone is cut through lengthwise. Afterwards it is closed again with wire loops.
116864.m: For a classic bypass operation, the breastbone is opened lengthwise.

a: An operation on the beating heart
An operation without a replacement vessel
116865.e: In the off-pump method no heart-lung machine is used. A stabiliser keeps the stitching site still on the beating heart.
116865.m: In an off-pump bypass the heart keeps beating during the operation.

116866.q: Which gentler treatment is often chosen instead of a bypass operation for narrowed coronary arteries?
a: A stent is inserted through a catheter
116866.e: Through a catheter in the groin or at the wrist, the narrowing is widened with a balloon and kept open with a stent. The chest does not have to be opened for this.
116866.m: A stent keeps a narrowed coronary artery open without major surgery.

116867.q: What does the German abbreviation ACVB stand for in heart surgery?
116867.e: ACVB refers to a bypass in which a vein leads from the aorta to the coronary artery beyond the narrowing. In English the operation is called CABG.
116867.m: An ACVB connects the aorta to a coronary artery via a vein.

116868.q: What is meant by heart failure?
a: The heart does not pump enough blood for the body's needs
The heart has a hole in the septum
The heart is wrapped in fat
116868.e: In heart failure the heart can no longer supply the body with enough blood, or only at raised filling pressures.
116868.m: In heart failure the heart's pumping power is not enough.

116869.q: Which symptom is typical of left-sided heart failure?
a: Breathlessness from congestion in the lungs
Strong thirst from high blood sugar
116869.e: If the left ventricle pumps too weakly, blood backs up into the lung vessels. Fluid leaks into the tissue, causing breathlessness and, in extreme cases, pulmonary oedema.
116869.m: A weak left ventricle leads to blood backing up in the lungs.

116870.q: Which sign points to right-sided heart failure?
a: Coughing up blood in the morning
116870.e: If the right ventricle pumps too weakly, blood backs up in the body's veins. This causes oedema in the legs, swollen neck veins and a congested liver.
116870.m: In right-sided heart failure, blood backs up in the body's veins.

116871.q: How can you tell severe heart failure from mild heart failure?
a: Breathlessness is present even at rest
Breathlessness only occurs during a marathon
There are no symptoms at all
116871.e: Doctors classify heart failure by its symptoms. In the most severe class, breathlessness and exhaustion are present even at rest.
116871.m: In severe heart failure, symptoms are present even at rest.

116872.q: What does the ejection fraction of the heart show?
a: The share of blood the ventricle pumps out per beat
The number of heartbeats per minute
The blood pressure in the aorta
The size of the heart in centimetres
116872.e: The ejection fraction shows what percentage of its filling the left ventricle pumps out in one beat. In healthy people it is over 50 per cent.
116872.m: The ejection fraction measures the pumping strength of the ventricle.

116873.q: Which examination assesses the heart's pumping power without an invasive procedure?
116873.e: A heart ultrasound shows the ventricles and valves moving. This makes it possible to estimate how strongly the heart pumps.
116873.m: A heart ultrasound shows how well the heart pumps.

116874.q: Why should people with heart failure weigh themselves every day?
a: A rapid gain shows fluid retention
They have to lose weight every day
116874.e: A gain of more than about 1 kg per day or 2 kg in a few days usually points to fluid in the body. The treatment must then be adjusted.
116874.m: Sudden weight gain can show that heart failure is getting worse.

116875.q: Which group of medicines flushes out water in heart failure?
116875.e: Diuretics increase the excretion of salt and water through the kidneys. This reduces oedema and breathlessness.
116875.m: Diuretics help get rid of excess water.

116876.q: From which plant does the historical heart medicine digitalis come?
116876.e: In 1785 the English doctor William Withering described the effect of foxglove leaves on dropsy. The active substances increase the strength of the heart.

a: The electrical activity of the heart
The blood pressure in the arteries
The size of the heart's ventricles
116877.e: The electrocardiogram uses electrodes on the skin to measure the electrical signals that trigger each heartbeat. This makes rhythm disorders such as atrial fibrillation visible.
116877.m: An ECG records the heart's electrical signals.

116878.q: Which serious complication is a particular risk with atrial fibrillation?
a: A stroke caused by a clot
116878.e: In the fibrillating atria, especially the left atrial appendage, blood flows slowly and can clot. A clot that breaks free can block an artery in the brain.
116878.m: Atrial fibrillation increases the risk of stroke.

116879.q: What is typically noticeable when feeling the pulse of someone with atrial fibrillation?
a: The pulse is very slow and completely regular
No pulse can be felt at all
The pulse always beats exactly 60 times a minute
116879.e: The atria twitch chaotically and the ventricles receive the signals at irregular intervals. That is why the pulse is completely irregular.
116879.m: Atrial fibrillation makes the pulse irregular.

116880.q: Which medicines do many people with atrial fibrillation take to prevent a stroke?
116880.e: Blood clots can form in the fibrillating atria. Anticoagulants make this less likely and so lower the risk of stroke.
116880.m: Blood thinners protect against stroke in atrial fibrillation.

a: A targeted electric shock that normalises the rhythm
An operation on the heart valves
116881.e: Under a short anaesthetic, an electric shock synchronised with the ECG is given. All cells are excited at the same time, and afterwards the sinus node often takes over again.
116881.m: Cardioversion uses an electric shock to put the heart back into sinus rhythm.

116882.q: Which structure sets the rhythm in the healthy heart, which is disturbed in atrial fibrillation?
116882.e: The sinus node in the right atrium is the natural pacemaker. In atrial fibrillation, chaotic excitation in the atria drowns out its rhythm.
116882.m: Normally the sinus node sets the heart's rhythm.

116883.q: Which factors particularly increase the risk of atrial fibrillation?
a: Older age and high blood pressure
Young age and a low pulse
116883.e: Atrial fibrillation becomes much more common with age. High blood pressure, being overweight, diabetes and a lot of alcohol also raise the risk.
116883.m: Age and high blood pressure are important risk factors for atrial fibrillation.

116884.q: How common is atrial fibrillation compared with other persistent heart rhythm disorders?
a: It is one of the rarest
116884.e: Atrial fibrillation is the most common persistent heart rhythm disorder. The risk rises clearly with age.
116884.m: Atrial fibrillation is the most common persistent heart rhythm disorder.

116885.q: Roughly how long does the battery of a modern pacemaker last?
116885.e: Modern pacemakers use very little power. When the battery runs out, the whole device is replaced in a small procedure.
116885.m: A pacemaker usually lasts about a decade.

116886.q: For which disorder is a pacemaker typically fitted?
a: A heartbeat that is too slow
116886.e: A pacemaker gives off electrical impulses when the heart beats too slowly, for example with AV block or sinus node disease.
116886.m: A pacemaker mainly helps when the heartbeat is too slow.

116887.q: What should people with a pacemaker watch out for in everyday life?
a: Not holding strong magnets or mobile phones directly over the device
116887.e: Strong magnetic fields can disturb how the pacemaker works. That is why mobile phones or headphones with magnets are kept a little way from the device.
116887.m: A pacemaker needs to be kept away from strong magnets.

116888.q: Which type of battery is usually used in modern pacemakers?
116888.e: Lithium batteries are small, very long-lasting and hardly discharge by themselves. With them, a pacemaker usually lasts many years.
116888.m: Pacemakers are usually powered by lithium batteries.

116889.q: By which route do the leads of a classic pacemaker reach the heart?
a: Through a vein below the collarbone
Through the aorta from the groin
Through the skin directly into the heart
116889.e: The leads are pushed through a vein below the collarbone into the right atrium or right ventricle. The device lies under the skin.
116889.m: Pacemaker leads are guided through a vein into the right side of the heart.

116890.q: What is special about a capsule pacemaker?
a: It sits directly in the right ventricle without wires
It is worn on the wrist
It is swallowed and passed out again
116890.e: The wireless capsule pacemaker is about the size of a large vitamin capsule and is placed in the right ventricle by catheter. No lead wires are then needed.
116890.m: A capsule pacemaker needs no wires.

116891.q: What is a biventricular pacemaker (CRT) for?
a: It synchronises both ventricles in heart failure
It dissolves blood clots in the atrium
It replaces a faulty heart valve
116891.e: In some forms of heart failure the ventricles contract out of step. Cardiac resynchronisation therapy stimulates both ventricles at the same time and so improves pumping.
116891.m: CRT brings both ventricles back into step.

116892.q: What can an implantable defibrillator (ICD) do in addition to a pacemaker?
a: End ventricular fibrillation with a shock
116892.e: An ICD recognises life-threatening fast rhythm disorders such as ventricular fibrillation and then gives an electric shock.
116892.m: An ICD can end ventricular fibrillation with an electric shock.

116893.q: With classic cold storage, roughly how long may a donor heart be outside the body?
116893.e: When cooled on ice, the heart should usually be supplied with blood again within about four hours. That is why removal, transport and implantation must happen very quickly.
116893.m: A donor heart must be implanted within a few hours.

116894.q: In which city did the world's first heart transplant take place in 1967?
116894.e: In December 1967 the surgeon Christiaan Barnard transplanted a human heart for the first time in Cape Town. Switzerland followed in 1969 in Zurich.
116894.m: The first heart transplant was carried out in Cape Town in 1967.

116895.q: Why do people have to take medicines for life after a heart transplant?
a: So that the immune system does not reject the donor heart
So that the heart grows faster
So that the blood becomes thicker
So that the scar heals more neatly
116895.e: The immune system recognises the donor heart as foreign. Medicines damp down the defence so that it does not attack the heart.
116895.m: After a transplant, medicines prevent rejection.

116896.q: Why does a transplanted heart react to exertion with a faster pulse only after a delay?
a: It is not connected to nerves
It is smaller than the old heart
116896.e: The nerves are cut during the transplant. So the heart only speeds up once hormones such as adrenaline rise in the blood.
116896.m: A transplanted heart is controlled mainly by hormones.

116897.q: How is rejection of a donor heart often monitored?
a: With small tissue samples from the heart muscle
116897.e: In an endomyocardial biopsy, tiny samples are taken from the inner wall of the heart through a catheter. Signs of rejection can be seen under the microscope.
116897.m: Heart muscle biopsies show the start of rejection.

116898.q: From which animal did the heart come that was transplanted into a living human for the first time in the USA in 2022?
116898.e: In January 2022, a man with severe heart disease in Maryland received a genetically modified pig heart. He lived for about two more months.
116898.m: Transplanting animal organs into humans is called xenotransplantation.

116899.q: What is a ventricular assist device (VAD) often used for before a transplant?
a: To bridge the time until a donor heart is available
116899.e: An implanted pump supports the weakened ventricle. This lets people with severe heart disease bridge the often long wait for a donor heart.
116899.m: A VAD can bridge the wait for a donor heart.

116900.q: In a usual heart transplant, what happens to the diseased heart?
a: It is removed and replaced by the donor heart
It is repaired and put back
It is moved into the abdomen
It is frozen and returned later
116900.e: The diseased heart is taken out and the donor heart is sewn in its place. Specialists call this orthotopic transplantation.
116900.m: In a usual heart transplant, the donor heart replaces the old heart.

116901.q: Apart from the coronary arteries, in which vessel are stents also often used?
a: In the portal vein of the liver
In the skin veins of the hand
116901.e: Stents are also used for narrowings of the carotid artery and the leg and kidney arteries. Everywhere the aim is to restore blood flow.
116901.m: Stents keep open not only coronary arteries but other arteries too.

116902.q: How does the sympathetic nervous system affect the sinus node?
116902.e: Through noradrenaline the sympathetic system has a positive chronotropic effect. The pacemaker cells depolarise faster and the heart beats more quickly.
116902.m: The sympathetic nervous system speeds up the heartbeat.

116903.q: Roughly what share of cardiac output flows through the coronary arteries at rest?
116903.e: The heart makes up only about half a per cent of body weight but receives about 5 % of cardiac output. Even at rest it extracts a lot of the oxygen from the blood.
116903.m: The heart receives about five per cent of cardiac output for itself.

116974.q: Roughly how much water per second does a power station need for 100 MW with a 400 m head and 90 % efficiency (using g = 9.81 m/s²)?
116974.e: From P = η · ρ · g · h · Q it follows that Q = 10⁸ W / (0.9 · 1000 · 9.81 · 400) ≈ 28.3 m³/s.
116974.m: The output of a hydroelectric power station depends on the head and the flow rate.

a: A machine that pumps or generates electricity depending on its direction of rotation
A pump that only extracts groundwater
A turbine driven by the wind
116975.e: In many pumped storage stations the same machine works as a pump in one direction of rotation and as a turbine in the other. This saves space and money.
116975.m: A pump turbine can pump water uphill and generate electricity.

116976.q: A pumped storage station buys electricity for 5 centimes per kWh and sells it for 12 centimes per kWh, at 80 % efficiency. How much is left over per 100 kWh bought?
116976.e: Buying: 100 kWh · 5 centimes = 5 francs. Selling: 80 kWh · 12 centimes = 9.60 francs. That leaves 4.60 francs.
116976.m: Pumped storage pays off when the price difference makes up for the losses.

116977.q: Which energy company is the main shareholder of Kraftwerke Linth-Limmern?
116977.e: Kraftwerke Linth-Limmern AG is mostly owned by Axpo; the canton of Glarus holds a minority stake.
116977.m: Kraftwerke Linth-Limmern is mostly owned by Axpo.

116978.q: Which lake serves as the upper reservoir of the Limmern pumped storage station?
116978.e: Water is pumped from the Limmernsee up into the higher Muttsee. When electricity is needed, it flows back down.
116978.m: The Muttsee is the upper reservoir of Limmern.

116979.q: Roughly how big is the difference in height between the Limmernsee and the Muttsee?
116979.e: According to the operator Axpo, the Muttsee lies just over 600 m higher than the Limmernsee.
116979.m: There are just over 600 metres of height between the Muttsee and the Limmernsee.

116980.q: Roughly how long is the dam at the Muttsee?
116980.e: The crest of the Muttsee dam is 1054 m long. According to Axpo, it is the longest dam in Switzerland.
116980.m: The Muttsee dam is over a kilometre long.

116981.q: How many pump turbines of 250 MW each are in the machine cavern at Limmern?
116981.e: Four machine sets stand in a cavern about 150 m long deep inside the mountain. Each machine can pump or generate electricity.
116981.m: Four large pump turbines work at Limmern.

116982.q: Roughly how much did it cost to build the Limmern pumped storage station?
116982.e: According to Axpo, the costs were about 2.1 billion francs, with a construction period of about seven years.
116982.m: Limmern is one of the most expensive power station projects in Switzerland.

116983.q: Roughly how much water per second is needed to generate 500 MW with a 600 m head and 90 % efficiency (using g = 9.81 m/s²)?
116983.m: Large outputs need an enormous flow of water, even with a high head.

116984.q: The Muttsee holds about 23 million m³. How much energy would it theoretically correspond to if this amount flowed 600 m down (using g = 9.81 m/s²)?
116984.e: E = 23 · 10⁹ kg · 9.81 m/s² · 600 m ≈ 1.35 · 10¹⁴ J. Divided by 3.6 · 10¹² J per GWh, that gives about 38 GWh.
116984.m: A large mountain lake theoretically stores energy in the range of dozens of gigawatt hours.

116985.e: 1 eV is the energy a particle with one elementary charge gains when it passes through 1 V: 1.602 · 10⁻¹⁹ C · 1 V.
116985.m: An electronvolt is a tiny amount of energy for single particles.

116986.q: An electron passes through a voltage of 5000 V. How much energy does it gain?
116986.e: A particle with one elementary charge gains 1 eV per volt. At 5000 V that is 5000 eV = 5 keV.
116986.m: An electron gains one electronvolt for every volt it passes through.

116987.q: An alpha particle (charge 2e) passes through 1000 V. How much energy does it gain?
116987.m: The energy gained in eV is the charge number times the voltage.

116988.m: Mega means one million, so one million electronvolts.

116989.q: What energy per beam have protons reached in the LHC at CERN near Geneva since 2022 (as of 2025)?
116989.e: In the third run, protons are accelerated to 6.8 TeV. In head-on collisions this gives 13.6 TeV.
116989.m: The LHC at CERN accelerates protons to teraelectronvolt energies.

116990.q: Roughly how large is the rest energy of a proton?
116990.e: According to E = m · c², the proton mass of 1.673 · 10⁻²⁷ kg corresponds to an energy of about 938 MeV, just under 1 GeV.
116990.m: A proton has a rest energy of just under one gigaelectronvolt.

116991.q: Roughly how large is the rest energy of an electron?
116991.e: According to E = m · c², the electron mass of 9.11 · 10⁻³¹ kg corresponds to an energy of about 511 keV.
116991.m: The rest energy of the electron is about half an MeV.

116993.q: What does the gravimetric energy density of an energy source tell you?
116993.e: Gravimetric energy density measures how much energy is contained in one kilogram, for example in kWh/kg or MJ/kg. Volumetric energy density refers to the volume.
116993.m: Energy density tells you how much energy is contained in a mass or a volume.

116994.q: Which energy source has the most energy per kilogram?
116994.e: Hydrogen has a calorific value of about 120 MJ/kg, almost three times as much as petrol with about 42 MJ/kg. Batteries store much less per kilogram.
116994.m: Hydrogen has the highest energy density per mass.

116995.q: A battery weighs 500 kg and has an energy density of 0.2 kWh/kg. How much energy does it store?
116995.m: Stored energy is mass times energy density.

116996.q: A tank holds 40 l of petrol with 8.8 kWh per litre. How much chemical energy is that?
116996.m: Petrol stores a lot of energy in a small volume.

116997.q: How many kilograms of water must be pumped up 500 m to store 1 kWh (using g = 9.81 m/s²)?
116997.m: The potential energy of water has a very low energy density.

116998.q: A vehicle battery stores 60 kWh and weighs 400 kg. What is its energy density?
116998.e: Energy density = energy / mass = 60 kWh / 400 kg = 0.15 kWh/kg.
116998.m: You get the energy density by dividing the energy by the mass.

116999.q: Why is hydrogen strongly compressed in vehicle tanks?
a: It has a low energy density per volume
116999.e: As a gas at normal pressure, hydrogen takes up a lot of space. That is why it is usually stored at 700 bar in vehicles.
116999.m: Hydrogen is rich in energy per mass but poor in energy per volume.

117000.q: A house needs 20,000 kWh of heat per year, and wood supplies about 4 kWh per kg. How much wood is needed without losses?
117000.e: m = 20,000 kWh / 4 kWh/kg = 5000 kg, so about 5 tonnes.
117000.m: The fuel mass needed is the energy demand divided by the energy density.

117001.q: What is the ionisation energy of a hydrogen atom in its ground state?
117001.e: To remove the electron completely from the ground state of the hydrogen atom takes 13.6 eV. This follows from the Bohr model of the atom and agrees with measurements.
117001.m: Atomic binding energies are in the range of a few electronvolts.

117002.q: A cyclist pedals at a constant 200 W for one hour. How much work does he do?

117200.q: In which blood vessels is blood pressure highest?
a: In the large arteries close to the heart
In the veins of the feet
117200.e: The left ventricle pumps blood at high pressure into the aorta and the large arteries. On its way through the vessels the pressure keeps falling.
117200.m: Blood pressure is highest in the arteries close to the heart.

117201.q: What does the systolic blood pressure value refer to?
a: The highest pressure while the heart is pumping out blood
The lowest pressure in the filling phase
The pressure in the pulmonary veins
The pressure in the right atrium
117201.e: The systolic value is the peak pressure in the arteries when the left ventricle pumps out blood. The diastolic value is the lowest pressure in the relaxation phase.
117201.m: The systolic value is the upper blood pressure value.

117203.q: When measuring blood pressure by hand, what do you hear with the stethoscope in the crook of the elbow?
a: Sounds of blood flowing in the artery
117203.e: When the cuff pressure is slowly released, blood spurts through the squeezed artery. These sounds show the upper and lower blood pressure values.
117203.m: When measuring blood pressure, you hear blood flowing through the artery.

117204.q: According to the “Ohm's law” of the circulation, which two quantities determine mean blood pressure?
117204.e: Blood pressure roughly equals cardiac output times total peripheral resistance. If one of them rises, the pressure rises too.
117204.m: Blood pressure comes from cardiac output times vessel resistance.

117205.q: Mean arterial pressure is roughly the diastolic value plus one third of the difference to the systolic value. What is it at 120/80 mmHg?
117205.e: 80 + (120 minus 80) / 3 gives about 93 mmHg. The mean pressure is closer to the lower value because the heart spends longer relaxing than contracting.
117205.m: Mean pressure is closer to the diastolic than to the systolic value.

117206.q: The flow resistance of a vessel depends on the fourth power of the radius. By what factor does it rise if the radius is halved?
117206.e: Resistance is inversely proportional to r to the power of 4. If the radius is halved, resistance rises by 2 to the power of 4, that is 16 times.
117206.m: Even small narrowings of a vessel raise resistance a lot.

117207.q: Which hormone from the adrenal medulla makes blood pressure and pulse rise quickly under stress?
117207.e: Under stress the adrenal medulla releases adrenaline. It speeds up the heartbeat and narrows many blood vessels, so blood pressure rises.
117207.m: Adrenaline drives up blood pressure and pulse.

117208.q: Which organ is most important for regulating blood pressure in the long term?
117208.e: The kidney controls blood volume through the excretion of salt and water. In this way it determines blood pressure over days and weeks.
117208.m: The kidney regulates blood pressure in the long run.

117209.q: Which stimulus do baroreceptors in the vessel wall react to?
117209.e: Baroreceptors are stretch receptors. If blood pressure rises, the vessel wall is stretched more and they fire more often.
117209.m: Baroreceptors measure blood pressure through the stretching of the wall.

117210.q: Where are the most important pressure sensors (baroreceptors) for arterial blood pressure?
a: In the carotid artery and the aortic arch
In the veins of the legs
In the alveoli of the lungs
117210.e: The most important arterial baroreceptors sit at the fork of the carotid artery and in the aortic arch, so close to the heart and on the way to the brain.
117210.m: The carotid artery and aortic arch contain the most important pressure sensors.

117211.q: In which part of the brain is the cardiovascular centre that processes the signals from the baroreceptors?
117211.e: The cardiovascular centre lies in the medulla oblongata. There the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems are adjusted.
117211.m: The cardiovascular centre sits in the medulla oblongata.

117212.q: What does the baroreceptor reflex do when blood pressure suddenly rises?
117212.e: More stretch leads to more signals to the cardiovascular centre. It damps down the sympathetic system and activates the vagus, so heart rate and pressure fall.
117212.m: When pressure is high, the baroreceptor reflex slows the heart.

117213.q: By which route do the baroreceptors' signals reach the cardiovascular centre?
a: Through hormones in the blood to the kidney
Through the spinal cord to the cerebellum
Through the lymph to the spleen
117213.e: The baroreceptors send their signals through cranial nerves such as the vagus to the cardiovascular centre in the brainstem. This lets the body react within seconds.
117213.m: Baroreceptors report the pressure to the brainstem through nerves.

117214.q: Why can strong pressure on the side of the carotid artery slow the heart?
a: The pressure sensors wrongly report high blood pressure
The carotid artery is completely blocked
The heart gets too little oxygen
The larynx presses on the heart
117214.e: Pressure from outside stretches the wall of the carotid artery. The brain interprets this as a rise in blood pressure and slows the heart by reflex.
117214.m: Pressure on the carotid artery can slow the heart.

117215.q: Which kind of blood pressure regulation is the baroreceptor reflex mainly responsible for?
117215.e: The reflex evens out short-term fluctuations, for example when standing up. With permanently high pressure the receptors adjust to a higher level.
117215.m: The baroreceptor reflex acts quickly, but only in the short term.

117216.q: What happens to the baroreceptors when blood pressure is permanently raised?
117216.e: In chronic hypertension the set point of the baroreceptors shifts upwards. The high pressure is then no longer reported as a deviation.
117216.m: Baroreceptors get used to permanently high pressure.

117217.q: In which organ is the enzyme renin made?
117217.e: Renin is made by specialised cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus in the kidney. They sit on the arterioles leading into the glomeruli.

117218.q: Which stimulus mainly leads to the release of renin?
a: Falling blood pressure in the kidney
117218.e: If the pressure in the kidney vessels or the amount of salt at the macula densa falls, more renin is released. The sympathetic system also stimulates the release.
117218.m: Low pressure in the kidney triggers renin release.

117219.q: Which protein does renin split into angiotensin I?
117219.e: Renin splits angiotensinogen, which is made in the liver. This produces angiotensin I, which has hardly any effect yet.
117219.m: Renin cuts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.

117220.q: Which enzyme converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II?
117220.e: ACE, mainly on the lining of the lung vessels, turns angiotensin I into the highly effective angiotensin II.
117220.m: ACE produces the active angiotensin II.

117221.e: Aldosterone is made in the outermost layer of the adrenal cortex, the zona glomerulosa. Angiotensin II stimulates its production.
117221.m: Aldosterone comes from the adrenal cortex.

117222.q: What does aldosterone do in the kidney tubules?
117222.e: In the collecting duct, aldosterone promotes the reabsorption of sodium and the excretion of potassium. Water follows the sodium, and blood volume rises.
117222.m: Aldosterone keeps sodium, and with it water, in the body.

117223.q: Which side effect is typical of ACE inhibitors?
a: A green discolouration of the skin
Loss of the sense of smell
117223.e: ACE also breaks down bradykinin. If it is inhibited, bradykinin builds up, which often triggers a dry cough.
117223.m: ACE inhibitors often cause an irritating cough.

117224.q: How do blood pressure medicines of the sartan group work?
a: They block the angiotensin II receptor
They inhibit renin production in the liver
117224.e: Sartans such as losartan occupy the AT1 receptor. Angiotensin II can then no longer narrow the vessels.
117224.m: Sartans protect the vessels from angiotensin II.

117225.q: From which natural model was the first ACE inhibitor, captopril, developed?
a: From the venom of a lancehead viper
117225.e: Peptides that inhibit ACE were found in the venom of the Brazilian snake Bothrops jararaca. They served as the model for captopril.
117225.m: A snake venom led to ACE inhibitors.

117226.q: From which values measured at the doctor's surgery does the usual European definition speak of high blood pressure?
117226.e: According to European guidelines, a value of 140/90 mmHg or more measured repeatedly at the surgery counts as hypertension. Values below that can still be raised.
117226.m: From 140/90 mmHg it is called high blood pressure.

117227.q: Why is high blood pressure often called a “silent killer”?
a: It causes no symptoms for a long time
117227.e: Many people affected feel nothing for years while their vessels, heart and kidneys are already being damaged. That is why regular measurements are important.
117227.m: High blood pressure often does harm without causing pain.

117228.q: What is the most common form of high blood pressure without a single identifiable cause called?
117228.e: In about nine out of ten people affected, no single cause is found. This is called primary or essential hypertension.
117228.m: Most high blood pressure has no single cause.

117229.q: Which organ can cause secondary hypertension if it makes too much aldosterone?
117229.e: The adrenal cortex makes the hormone aldosterone. If there is too much of it, the body holds back sodium and water and blood pressure rises.
117229.m: Too much aldosterone from the adrenal gland raises blood pressure.

117230.q: How does the left ventricle react to years of raised blood pressure?
a: It shrinks to the size of an atrium
117230.e: The heart constantly has to pump against higher pressure. The muscle grows as with training, causing left ventricular hypertrophy.
117230.m: High blood pressure thickens the wall of the left ventricle.

117231.q: Which dietary measure has been shown to lower blood pressure in many people?
117231.e: A lot of sodium binds water in the body and so increases blood volume. A diet lower in salt lowers blood pressure in many people affected.
117231.m: Less salt often helps against high blood pressure.

117232.q: What is 24-hour blood pressure monitoring for?
a: It shows the pattern over day and night
It measures the pressure in the lungs
117232.e: A portable device takes measurements at intervals all day and during the night. This reveals, for example, white coat hypertension or a missing fall in pressure at night.
117232.m: Long-term monitoring shows blood pressure in everyday life.

a: Very high blood pressure with acute organ damage
Slightly raised blood pressure without symptoms
A sudden drop in blood pressure
A high pulse with normal blood pressure
117233.e: In a hypertensive emergency, blood pressure is greatly raised and acutely damages organs such as the brain, heart or kidneys. It must be treated in hospital immediately.
117233.m: A hypertensive emergency needs immediate treatment.

117234.q: Which organ can be so damaged by years of high blood pressure that dialysis becomes necessary?
117234.e: High pressure damages the fine vessels of the renal corpuscles. In the long term kidney function can fall so much that blood cleaning by dialysis is needed.
117234.m: High blood pressure can destroy the kidneys.

117235.q: From which values do doctors usually speak of low blood pressure in adults?
117235.e: Values below about 100/60 mmHg usually count as hypotension. However, many people with such values have no symptoms.
117235.m: Low blood pressure is below about 100/60 mmHg.

117236.q: What is a drop in blood pressure that occurs when standing up quickly called?
117236.e: When you stand up, blood sinks into the legs. If the circulation reacts too slowly, the pressure falls and you feel dizzy.
117236.m: Dizziness on standing up comes from a drop in blood pressure.

117237.q: How does a doctor check whether the circulation reacts well when standing up?
a: Blood pressure and pulse are measured lying down and then standing
Temperature is measured before and after eating
The person is made to run for ten minutes
Blood sugar is measured while sitting
117237.e: In the so-called Schellong test, blood pressure and pulse lying down and standing are compared. If blood pressure drops sharply, there is an orthostatic disorder.
117237.m: A lying-standing test checks the circulation's reaction to standing up.

117238.q: What is a brief loss of consciousness due to a temporary lack of blood flow to the brain called?
117238.e: In a syncope, blood pressure briefly falls so much that the brain gets too little blood. Lying down, people usually recover quickly.
117238.m: The medical term for fainting is syncope.

117239.q: What helps many people with low blood pressure in everyday life?
a: Drinking enough and standing up slowly
Taking hot baths for as long as possible
Drinking little and standing up quickly
117239.e: Enough fluid increases blood volume. Standing up slowly gives the circulation time to adjust.
117239.m: Drinking and standing up slowly help with low blood pressure.

117240.q: Why can compression stockings help with low blood pressure?
a: They stop blood from pooling in the leg veins
117240.e: Pressure from outside reduces the diameter of the leg veins. This lets more blood flow back to the heart and keeps the pressure more stable.
117240.m: Compression stockings stop blood from staying in the legs.

117241.q: Which life-threatening condition with a sharp drop in blood pressure can develop after heavy blood loss?
117241.e: If a lot of blood volume is missing, the heart cannot pump out enough. Blood pressure falls and organs are no longer adequately supplied.
117241.m: Heavy blood loss can trigger shock.

117242.q: How does the body normally react to a drop in blood pressure on standing up?
a: The pulse rises and vessels narrow
The pulse falls and vessels widen
117242.e: Less stretching of the baroreceptors activates the sympathetic system. Heart rate and vessel tension increase, and blood pressure is maintained.
117242.m: When you stand up, the body speeds up the heart.

a: A blocked blood vessel in the brain
117244.e: About four out of five strokes are ischaemic. A blood clot blocks an artery in the brain, and the tissue beyond it no longer gets oxygen.
117244.m: A clot usually causes the stroke.

117245.q: In the FAST test, what does the letter T stand for?
a: The time until you call the emergency number
117245.e: FAST stands for Face, Arms, Speech and Time. The T reminds you to call the emergency number immediately, because every minute counts.
117245.m: With a stroke, every minute counts.

117246.q: What is a stroke called that is caused by a blood vessel in the brain bursting?
117246.e: In a haemorrhagic stroke, blood leaks into the brain tissue. The most common cause is blood pressure that has been too high for a long time.
117246.m: A brain haemorrhage is a haemorrhagic stroke.

117247.q: Which treatment dissolves the blood clot with medicines in an ischaemic stroke?
117247.e: In thrombolysis a substance that dissolves the clot is injected. It is only possible within a narrow time window after the symptoms begin.
117247.m: Thrombolysis dissolves clots in the brain.

117248.q: Up to how many hours after symptoms begin is thrombolysis usually possible for a stroke?
117248.e: Thrombolysis is usually used up to about 4.5 hours after symptoms begin. After that the risks of bleeding outweigh the benefits.
117248.m: There is only a little time for thrombolysis in a stroke.

117249.q: What is done in a mechanical thrombectomy?
a: The clot is pulled out with a catheter
Part of the skull is replaced
117249.e: Through a catheter from the groin, the clot is removed from the artery in the brain. The method is suitable for blockages of large vessels.
117249.m: In a thrombectomy the clot is taken out.

117250.q: Which heart rhythm disorder is a common cause of blood clots that trigger a stroke?
117250.e: In atrial fibrillation the atrium no longer contracts properly. Clots form in the still blood and can be washed into the brain.
117250.m: Atrial fibrillation increases the risk of stroke.

117251.q: What is a transient ischaemic attack?
a: Brief stroke symptoms that disappear quickly
117251.e: In a TIA, signs of a stroke appear that usually go away within minutes. It is considered an urgent warning sign of a coming stroke.
117251.m: A TIA is a serious warning signal.

117252.q: Where does the blood clot in a pulmonary embolism usually come from?
a: From a deep vein in the leg
117252.e: Usually a clot breaks free from a deep vein thrombosis in the leg or pelvis. It reaches the pulmonary arteries through the right side of the heart.
117252.m: Pulmonary embolisms usually begin in the leg veins.

117253.q: Through which ventricle of the heart does a clot from the leg veins reach the lungs?
117253.e: Venous blood flows through the vena cava into the right atrium and right ventricle. From there it is pumped into the pulmonary artery.
117253.m: A venous clot passes through the right side of the heart.

117254.q: Which set of symptoms is typical of a pulmonary embolism?
117254.e: Typical signs are sudden breathlessness, pain when breathing and a fast pulse. Large embolisms can lead to circulatory failure.
117254.m: Sudden breathlessness can point to a pulmonary embolism.

117255.q: Which factor encourages a thrombosis to form?
a: Good blood flow to the skin
117255.e: Rudolf Virchow named three causes: damage to the vessel wall, slowed blood flow and increased clotting of the blood. This is called Virchow's triad.

117256.q: Which blood test helps rule out a pulmonary embolism when suspicion is low?
117256.e: D-dimers are breakdown products of fibrin. If the value is normal and the probability is low, a pulmonary embolism is very unlikely.
117256.m: Normal D-dimers speak against a fresh thrombosis.

117257.q: Which imaging method is usually used today to detect a pulmonary embolism?
117257.e: In CT angiography contrast medium is injected. Clots in the pulmonary arteries then show up as gaps.
117257.m: CT angiography shows clots in the pulmonary arteries.

117258.q: Which group of medicines is the basis of treatment for a pulmonary embolism?
117258.e: Anticoagulants such as heparin stop the clot from growing and new ones from forming. The body can then break down the plug itself.
117258.m: Anticoagulants are the basis of embolism treatment.

117259.q: Why do long flights increase the risk of a pulmonary embolism?
a: Sitting for a long time slows blood flow in the legs
The high-altitude air thins the blood
The airline food thickens the blood
117259.e: When sitting for a long time the calf muscle pump hardly works and the veins are bent. The blood flows more slowly and clots more easily.
117259.m: On long journeys you should move your legs.

117260.q: Which group of substances does cholesterol belong to?
117260.e: Cholesterol is a sterol with the typical steroid skeleton of four rings. It belongs to the lipids.

117261.q: What job does cholesterol have in the cell membrane?
117261.e: Cholesterol slots in between the phospholipids. It makes the membrane more stable but not rigid.

117262.q: Which organ makes most of the body's own cholesterol?
117262.e: The liver is the most important place where cholesterol is made. The body makes more cholesterol itself than it takes in with food.

117263.q: What is the basic skeleton of the cholesterol molecule made of?
a: A long chain of amino acids
117263.e: Cholesterol has the typical steroid skeleton of four rings. All steroid hormones share this basic skeleton.
117263.m: Cholesterol has a skeleton of four rings.

117264.q: Which components of bile are made from cholesterol in the liver?
117264.e: The liver converts cholesterol into bile acids. In the gut these help to emulsify and absorb fats.
117264.m: The liver makes bile acids from cholesterol.

117265.q: What are medicines from the statin group used for?
a: To lower a cholesterol level that is too high
117265.e: Statins slow a key enzyme of cholesterol production in the liver. As a result LDL cholesterol in the blood falls and the risk of heart attacks decreases.

117266.q: Which stress hormone is made from cholesterol?
117266.e: Cortisol is a steroid hormone of the adrenal cortex. Like all steroid hormones, it is made from cholesterol.

117267.q: Why does cholesterol in the blood need transport particles?
a: It is hardly soluble in water
It is poisonous to blood cells
117267.e: Cholesterol is fat-soluble and does not dissolve in watery blood. It is therefore transported in lipoproteins with a coat of proteins and phospholipids.
117267.m: Cholesterol travels in the blood in lipoproteins.

117268.q: What does the abbreviation LDL stand for?
117268.e: LDL means low-density lipoprotein. Compared with its protein it contains a lot of fat and is therefore light.

117269.q: In which direction does LDL mainly transport cholesterol?
a: From the liver to the body's cells
From the body's cells to the liver
From the gut to the lungs
From the kidney to the gut
117269.e: LDL delivers cholesterol from the liver to the tissues. Too much of it can build up in vessel walls.
117269.m: LDL brings cholesterol to the cells.

117270.q: Why is LDL cholesterol often called “bad” cholesterol?
117270.e: A lot of LDL gets into the vessel wall and is altered there. It contributes to the formation of plaques and so to arteriosclerosis.
117270.m: A lot of LDL harms the arteries.

117271.q: How do cells take up LDL particles from the blood?
117271.e: The LDL receptor binds LDL on the cell surface. It is then taken in by endocytosis.
117271.m: The LDL receptor brings LDL into the cell.

117272.q: How do statins lower the LDL level in the blood?
a: They inhibit cholesterol production in the liver
They stop fat being absorbed in the stomach
117272.e: Statins slow a key enzyme of cholesterol production. The liver cells then make more LDL receptors and take more LDL out of the blood, as Brown and Goldstein showed.
117272.m: Statins lower LDL through the liver.

117273.q: Which hereditary disease with a faulty LDL receptor leads to very high LDL levels?
117273.e: In familial hypercholesterolaemia the LDL receptor works poorly. LDL stays in the blood, and heart attacks can occur early.
117273.m: A faulty LDL receptor raises LDL sharply.

117274.q: What are the eating cells in the vessel wall called that have stuffed themselves with oxidised LDL?
117274.e: Macrophages take up altered LDL and fill with fat droplets. Under the microscope they look foamy and form the core of early plaques.
117274.m: Foam cells are an early sign of arteriosclerosis.

117275.q: Roughly how is an LDL particle built?
a: A fatty core with a coat of protein and phospholipids
A red blood cell loaded with fat
117275.e: Fat does not dissolve in water. In LDL, cholesterol and fats lie inside, while phospholipids and the protein apolipoprotein B-100 sit on the outside.
117275.m: LDL is a ball of fat with a water-soluble coat.

117276.q: What does the abbreviation HDL stand for?
117276.e: HDL means high-density lipoprotein. It contains a relatively large amount of protein and little fat.

117277.q: What is the main job of HDL in fat metabolism?
a: Bringing cholesterol back to the liver
117277.e: HDL takes up excess cholesterol from tissues and vessel walls and brings it to the liver. This is called reverse cholesterol transport.
117277.m: HDL brings cholesterol back to the liver.

117278.q: Why is HDL cholesterol often called “good” cholesterol?
a: It removes cholesterol from the vessels
It supplies energy for the brain
117278.e: Because HDL carries cholesterol away from the vessel wall, higher levels are linked with less arteriosclerosis.
117278.m: HDL helps clear cholesterol from the vessels.

117279.q: Which lipoprotein is often called “bad” cholesterol?
117279.e: LDL brings cholesterol from the liver to the tissues. Too much LDL encourages deposits in the vessel walls.
117279.m: LDL counts as bad cholesterol, HDL as good cholesterol.

117280.q: Which lifestyle habit has been shown to raise HDL cholesterol?
117280.e: Endurance training raises the HDL level. Smoking and lack of exercise, on the other hand, lower it.

117281.q: What does a very low HDL level mean for cardiovascular risk?
117281.e: Low HDL levels count as a risk factor for arteriosclerosis. An important way of removing cholesterol from the vessels is missing.
117281.m: Little HDL is bad for the vessels.

117282.q: Which class of lipoprotein has the highest density?
117282.e: Density increases with the share of protein. HDL has the most protein, chylomicrons the most fat and the lowest density.
117282.m: The more protein, the denser the lipoprotein.

117283.q: What is a lipoprotein such as HDL?
a: A transport particle of protein and fat in the blood
An enzyme for digesting fat in the stomach
117283.e: Fats do not dissolve in water. That is why cholesterol and other fats are transported in the blood in particles with a coat of proteins.
117283.m: Lipoproteins transport fats in the blood.

117284.q: What job do venous valves have?
a: They stop blood from flowing backwards
They filter bacteria out of the blood
117284.e: Venous valves are pockets that only open towards the heart. If blood flows back, they close.
117284.m: Venous valves only let blood flow towards the heart.

117285.q: What is the mechanism called in which muscles squeeze the leg veins and press the blood towards the heart?
117285.e: When the leg muscles tense, they press on the deep veins. The valves make sure that the blood only flows upwards.
117285.m: When walking, the calf muscles pump blood to the heart.

117286.q: In which part of the body are there especially many venous valves?
117286.e: In the legs the blood has to flow upwards against gravity. That is why leg veins have many valves.
117286.m: The legs need especially many venous valves.

117287.q: Which condition often develops when the valves in the superficial leg veins no longer close?
117287.e: If the valves close poorly, blood backs up and the veins widen. Twisting varicose veins develop, medically called varices.
117287.m: Leaky venous valves lead to varicose veins.

117288.q: Which English doctor used the venous valves in 1628 as an argument for the circulation of the blood?
117288.e: William Harvey showed that the valves only let blood flow towards the heart. This supported his theory of a closed blood circulation.
117288.m: Harvey used the venous valves to prove the circulation.

117289.q: Which large veins have no venous valves?
117289.e: The superior and inferior vena cava have no valves. Here mainly the suction from breathing and the heart is at work.
117289.m: The venae cavae have no valves.

117290.q: What is the chronic disease with swelling and skin changes caused by damaged venous valves called?
117290.e: In chronic venous insufficiency, blood backs up in the legs. This leads to oedema, discolouration and in the worst case to a leg ulcer.
117290.m: Broken venous valves cause blood to back up in the legs.

117291.q: From which layer of the vessel wall are venous valves formed?
a: From the outer connective tissue layer
117291.e: Venous valves are folds of the intima, the innermost layer of the wall. They are covered with endothelium.
117291.m: Venous valves are folds of the vessel's inner lining.

a: A bypass route for the blood
The flow of lymph in the gut
117292.e: If a vessel is narrowed or blocked, blood can flow through side vessels. This bypass is called collateral circulation.

117293.q: Why does a blockage of one carotid artery not always lead to a stroke?
a: A ring of vessels at the base of the brain redirects blood
The neck veins take over the supply
The heart then beats twice as fast
117293.e: The circle of Willis at the base of the brain connects the carotid arteries and the vertebral arteries. If one supply fails, blood can be redirected through this ring.
117293.m: The circle of Willis secures the brain's blood supply.

117294.q: What can form when blood backs up in front of a scarred liver?
a: A hole in the septum of the heart
117294.e: In cirrhosis of the liver, blood backs up in the portal vein. It takes a detour through veins of the oesophagus, which widen into varices and can bleed heavily.
117294.m: Blood backing up in front of the liver can cause varicose veins in the oesophagus.

117295.q: Why can thick veins sometimes be seen on the belly when blood backs up badly in front of the liver?
a: The blood looks for detours past the liver
The stomach muscles push the veins outwards
The skin becomes thinner and transparent
The heart pumps too little blood into the legs
117295.e: If blood cannot flow through the liver, it takes a detour through veins in the skin of the belly. These widen in a star shape around the navel; this picture is called caput medusae.
117295.m: Widened belly veins show a bypass circulation around the liver.

117296.q: With an inborn narrowing of the aorta, the pulse in the legs is often weak. Why?
a: Less blood arrives beyond the narrowing
The leg muscles need no oxygen
117296.e: In coarctation of the aorta, the main artery is narrowed after the arm arteries branch off. The arms get plenty of blood, the legs less; bypasses through the rib arteries only partly make up for this.
117296.m: A narrowing in the aorta reduces blood flow to the legs.

117297.q: What happens to small connecting arteries when a large artery slowly narrows?
a: They grow into larger bypass vessels
117297.e: When more blood flows through small connecting arteries, they grow into effective collaterals. This remodelling is called arteriogenesis.
117297.m: Small arteries can grow into bypass vessels.

117298.q: Which stimulus particularly encourages collaterals to grow?
a: Increased blood flow and shear stress
117298.e: If more blood flows through the side routes after a narrowing, the vessel walls feel greater shear stress. This stimulates their growth.
117298.m: More blood flow makes collaterals grow.

117299.q: Why is a blockage that develops slowly often milder than a sudden one?
a: There is time for collaterals to form
117299.e: With a slow narrowing, bypass vessels can develop. With a sudden blockage they are missing and the tissue dies faster.
117299.m: Slow narrowings give collaterals time to grow.

117300.q: In which SI unit is torque given?
117300.e: Torque is the product of lever arm and force. This gives the unit N·m, the newton metre.
117300.m: Torque is measured in newton metres.

117301.q: A force of 50 N acts at right angles on a lever 0.4 m long. How large is the torque?
117301.e: With a perpendicular force, M = r · F. 0.4 m · 50 N gives 20 N·m.
117301.m: Torque is lever arm times perpendicular force.

117302.q: A force of 100 N acts 0.5 m from the axis of rotation at an angle of 30° to the lever. How large is the torque?
117302.e: Only the perpendicular part of the force counts: M = r · F · sin(30°). 0.5 m · 100 N · 0.5 gives 25 N·m.
117302.m: Only the perpendicular component of a force produces torque.

117303.q: In which direction does the torque vector point?
a: Perpendicular to the lever arm and the force
117303.e: Torque is the cross product of the position vector and the force. It is perpendicular to both, and the right-hand rule gives the direction.
117303.m: The torque vector points along the axis of rotation.

117304.q: Why is the door handle placed as far as possible from the hinges?
a: A long lever arm needs less force
It makes the door close faster
117304.e: For the same turning effect, a smaller force is enough if you are further from the pivot. That is why a door is easy to open at its outer edge.
117304.m: A long lever arm saves force.

117305.q: A wheel nut is to be tightened to 60 N·m. What force is needed at right angles at the end of a spanner 0.25 m long?
117305.e: From M = r · F it follows that F = M / r. 60 N·m divided by 0.25 m gives 240 N.
117305.m: With a shorter spanner you need more force.

117306.q: Two equal and opposite forces of 30 N each act 0.2 m apart along parallel lines. How large is the torque of this couple?
117306.e: A couple produces a torque equal to the force times the distance between the lines of action. 30 N · 0.2 m gives 6 N·m.

117307.q: An engine delivers a torque of 200 N·m at 3000 revolutions per minute. Roughly what power does it produce?
117307.e: P = M · ω. 3000 per minute is 50 per second, so ω = 2π · 50 ≈ 314 rad/s. 200 N·m · 314 rad/s gives about 63 kW.
117307.m: Power is torque times angular velocity.

117308.q: When does a force produce no torque about an axis, even though it is large?
a: When its line of action passes through the axis
When it is perpendicular to the lever
When the lever is very long
117308.e: If the line of action passes through the axis of rotation, the effective lever arm is zero. Then the cross product vanishes.
117308.m: No lever arm means no torque.

117309.q: Which quantity of straight-line motion corresponds to the moment of inertia in rotational motion?
117309.e: The moment of inertia describes how strongly a body resists a change in its rotation. It plays the same role as mass does in translation.
117309.m: The moment of inertia is the mass of rotational motion.

117310.q: Apart from its mass, what does the moment of inertia of a body depend on?
a: How the mass is distributed around the axis
117310.e: The further mass is from the axis of rotation, the more it contributes, because it counts with the square of the distance. The same body therefore has different moments of inertia for different axes.
117310.m: Mass far from the axis greatly increases the moment of inertia.

117311.q: A point mass of 2 kg circles an axis at a distance of 0.5 m. What is its moment of inertia?
117311.e: For a point mass, J = m · r². 2 kg · (0.5 m)² gives 0.5 kg·m².
117311.m: For a point mass: mass times distance squared.

117312.q: What is the moment of inertia of a thin-walled hollow cylinder of mass m and radius r about its axis of symmetry?
117312.e: In a thin-walled hollow cylinder all the mass lies at a distance r from the axis. So J = m · r².
117312.m: In a hollow cylinder all the mass is on the outside.

117313.q: A solid cylinder has a mass of 4 kg and a radius of 0.5 m. What is its moment of inertia about its axis of symmetry?
117313.e: For a solid cylinder, J = ½ · m · r². ½ · 4 kg · 0.25 m² gives 0.5 kg·m².
117313.m: A solid cylinder has a moment of inertia of one half m r squared.

117314.q: A solid sphere and a thin-walled hollow cylinder with the same mass and radius roll down a slope at the same time. Which one reaches the bottom first?
a: It depends only on the mass
117314.e: In the hollow cylinder all the mass is on the outside, so it has the larger moment of inertia. It needs more energy for rotation and therefore rolls more slowly.
117314.m: The smaller the moment of inertia, the faster a body rolls.

117315.q: A thin rod of 6 kg and 2 m in length rotates about an axis through its centre. Its moment of inertia is J = m · l² / 12. How large is J?
117315.e: Putting in the values gives J = 6 kg · 4 m² / 12 = 2 kg·m².
117315.m: A rod about its centre has one twelfth m l squared.

117316.q: A torque of 10 N·m acts on a body with a moment of inertia of 2 kg·m². What is the angular acceleration?
117316.e: The basic equation of rotation is M = J · α. So α = 10 N·m / 2 kg·m² = 5 rad/s².
117316.m: Torque is moment of inertia times angular acceleration.

117317.q: What is the SI unit of the moment of inertia?
117317.e: The moment of inertia is a sum of masses times squared distances. This gives the unit kilogram times square metre.
117317.m: The moment of inertia has the unit kilogram times square metre.

117318.q: Which physicist proposed a model of the atom in 1913 in which the angular momentum of electrons can only take certain values?
117318.e: In Bohr's model of 1913, electrons may only orbit on paths whose angular momentum is a whole-number multiple of h / 2π. This is how Bohr explained the spectral lines of hydrogen.
117318.m: Niels Bohr introduced quantised electron orbits.

117319.q: A wheel with a moment of inertia of 0.4 kg·m² rotates at 10 rad/s. What is its angular momentum?
117319.e: L = J · ω = 0.4 kg·m² · 10 rad/s = 4 kg·m²/s.
117319.m: Faster rotation means more angular momentum.

117320.q: A mass of 0.2 kg moves at 3 m/s on a circle with a radius of 0.5 m. What is its angular momentum about the centre of the circle?
117320.e: For a point mass on a circular path, L = r · m · v. 0.5 m · 0.2 kg · 3 m/s gives 0.3 kg·m²/s.
117320.m: A point mass on a circular path also has angular momentum.

117321.q: A constant torque of 2 N·m acts on a wheel for 3 seconds. By how much does its angular momentum change?
117321.e: Torque is the rate of change of angular momentum. ΔL = M · Δt = 2 N·m · 3 s = 6 kg·m²/s.

117322.q: Which constant of nature has the same unit as angular momentum?
117322.e: The Planck constant has the unit joule second, which equals kg·m²/s. In quantum mechanics, angular momenta occur in multiples of it.
117322.m: Angular momenta in atoms are quantised.

117323.q: What is the intrinsic angular momentum of elementary particles such as the electron called?
117323.e: Spin is an internal angular momentum that particles have without any classical rotation. For the electron it is ½ in units of ħ.
117323.m: Spin is the intrinsic angular momentum of a particle.

117324.q: How do you find the direction of the angular momentum vector of a spinning wheel?
a: With the right-hand rule along the axis
It always points to the centre of the Earth
It points in the direction the rim moves
117324.e: If you curl the fingers of your right hand in the direction of rotation, your thumb points in the direction of the angular momentum. It lies on the axis of rotation.
117324.m: Angular momentum points along the axis of rotation.

117325.q: Why does a fast-spinning top not fall over straight away?
a: Its angular momentum stabilises the direction of its axis
It is lighter than a top at rest
The air holds it up from below
The Earth pulls on it less strongly
117325.e: A large angular momentum can only be changed by a torque. So gravity does not tip the top over but makes its axis slowly circle around.
117325.m: Angular momentum stabilises the axis of rotation.

117326.q: Under what condition is the angular momentum of a system conserved?
a: When there is no internal friction
When the mass does not move
117326.e: Only an external torque can change the total angular momentum. The effects of internal forces cancel out.
117326.m: Without an external torque, angular momentum stays the same.

117327.q: Why does a figure skater spin faster when she pulls her arms in to her body?
a: Her moment of inertia falls while her angular momentum stays the same
117327.e: With her arms pulled in, her mass is closer to the axis of rotation, so the moment of inertia gets smaller. Since J · ω stays constant, the angular velocity rises.
117327.m: Pulling in your arms makes a pirouette faster.

117328.q: A skater spins at 2 revolutions per second and reduces her moment of inertia from 4 to 1.6 kg·m². How fast does she spin afterwards?
117328.e: From J₁ · ω₁ = J₂ · ω₂ it follows that ω₂ = 4 · 2 / 1.6 = 5 revolutions per second.
117328.m: Halving the moment of inertia doubles the rate of spin.

117329.q: Where does the extra rotational energy come from when a figure skater pulls in her arms during a pirouette?
a: From the work done by her muscles
117329.e: The angular momentum stays the same, but the rotational energy L² / (2J) increases. The skater supplies the difference by pulling her arms inwards against the centrifugal force.
117329.m: Pulling in your arms means doing work.

117330.q: Which of Kepler's laws follows directly from the conservation of angular momentum?
a: The second, the law of equal areas
117330.e: The Sun's gravity acts towards the centre and produces no torque. So the line from the Sun to the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times.
117330.m: The law of equal areas is conservation of angular momentum.

117331.q: Why do neutron stars often rotate extremely fast?
a: Their radius shrinks hugely when they collapse
117331.e: When a star's core collapses, its radius becomes enormously smaller. With angular momentum conserved, the rate of spin rises, up to hundreds of revolutions per second.

117332.q: What is the tail rotor of a helicopter with one main rotor for?
a: It stops the body from turning against the rotor
117332.e: When the engine drives the main rotor, an equal counter-torque acts on the body. The tail rotor produces an opposing torque and keeps the body steady.
117332.m: The tail rotor balances the counter-torque.

117333.q: A person sits on a swivel chair holding a spinning wheel with a vertical axis. What happens when they turn the wheel upside down?
117333.e: The wheel's angular momentum is reversed. To keep the total angular momentum the same, the person and chair must turn in the direction the wheel was originally spinning.
117333.m: Turning a wheel over sets the swivel chair spinning.

117334.q: How can a falling cat turn in the air to land on its feet, even though its total angular momentum stays zero?
a: It twists its front and back body against each other
It pushes off against the air
117334.e: The cat twists its front and back body in turn and changes the moments of inertia as it does so. This lets it change its position without the total angular momentum moving away from zero.
117334.m: Internal movements let you turn without gaining angular momentum.

117335.q: What is Steiner's theorem (the parallel axis theorem) for an axis at distance d parallel to the axis through the centre of mass?
117335.e: The moment of inertia about the shifted axis is the moment of inertia about the centre of mass plus mass times distance squared. Both axes must be parallel.
117335.m: Steiner's theorem adds mass times distance squared.

117336.q: From which present-day Swiss canton did the mathematician Jakob Steiner, after whom the theorem is named, come?
117336.e: Jakob Steiner was born in 1796 in Utzenstorf in the canton of Bern. He later became a professor in Berlin and is known above all for his geometry.
117336.m: Jakob Steiner was a mathematician from Bern.

117337.q: A thin rod of 3 kg and 2 m in length rotates about an axis through one end, at right angles to the rod. What is its moment of inertia?
117337.e: About the centre, J_S = 3 · 4 / 12 = 1 kg·m². The distance to the end is 1 m, so J = 1 + 3 · 1² = 4 kg·m².
117337.m: A rod is harder to turn about its end than about its centre.

117338.q: For which position of the axis of rotation is the moment of inertia smallest among all parallel axes?
a: For the axis through the centre of mass
For the axis at the edge of the body
It is the same for all axes
117338.e: According to Steiner's theorem, m · d² is always added to the value for the centre of mass. This addition is only zero when d = 0.
117338.m: The moment of inertia is smallest through the centre of mass.

117339.q: A solid cylinder of 2 kg with a radius of 0.1 m rotates about an axis on its curved surface, parallel to its axis of symmetry. What is its moment of inertia?
117339.e: J_S = ½ · 2 · 0.01 = 0.01 kg·m². Steiner adds 2 · 0.1² = 0.02 kg·m², making 0.03 kg·m² in total.
117339.m: A rolling cylinder momentarily turns about the line where it touches the ground.

117340.q: A solid sphere of 1 kg with a radius of 0.1 m has a moment of inertia of 0.004 kg·m² about its centre. What is it about a tangent to its surface?
117340.e: Steiner adds m · d² = 1 · 0.1² = 0.01 kg·m². Together that gives 0.004 + 0.01 = 0.014 kg·m².
117340.m: Steiner's theorem also works for spheres.

117341.q: A body of 2 kg has a moment of inertia of 0.1 kg·m² about the axis through its centre of mass. What is it about a parallel axis 0.3 m away?
117341.e: According to Steiner, J = J_S + m · d². 0.1 + 2 · 0.3² = 0.1 + 0.18 gives 0.28 kg·m².
117341.m: The Steiner part grows with the square of the distance.

117342.q: Which condition must be met to apply Steiner's theorem?
a: One of the axes passes through the centre of mass
Both axes are at right angles to each other
The body must be at rest
117342.e: The theorem links any axis with the parallel axis through the centre of mass. It does not apply directly between two arbitrary parallel axes.
117342.m: Steiner's theorem needs an axis through the centre of mass.

117343.q: How did the gyrobus made by Maschinenfabrik Oerlikon store its driving energy?
117343.e: At charging stations an electric motor sped up the flywheel. While driving, it gave its rotational energy back as electrical energy to the traction motor.
117343.m: The gyrobus ran on the rotational energy of a flywheel.

117344.q: A body with J = 2 kg·m² rotates at 3 rad/s. What is its rotational energy?
117344.m: For rotational energy you square the angular velocity.

117345.q: How does rotational energy change when the angular velocity doubles?
117345.e: Since ω is squared, doubling it gives a factor of 2² = 4.
117345.m: Twice the rate of spin means four times the rotational energy.

117346.q: What do you call a rotating mass that is used to store energy?
117346.e: A flywheel stores energy as rotational energy and releases it again when it slows down. It smooths the running of engines, for example.
117346.m: A flywheel stores energy in its rotation.

117347.q: What fraction of the total kinetic energy of a rolling solid cylinder is rotational energy?
117347.e: Translation: ½ · m · v². Rotation: ½ · ½ · m · r² · (v/r)² = ¼ · m · v². So of the total ¾ · m · v², one third is rotational energy.
117347.m: In a rolling solid cylinder, one third of the energy is in the rotation.

117348.q: A solid sphere and a thin-walled hollow sphere of the same mass and size roll down the same slope. Which reaches the bottom first?
117348.e: The hollow sphere has a larger moment of inertia and puts more energy into rotation. So the solid sphere becomes faster.
117348.m: The solid sphere wins the rolling race against the hollow sphere.

117349.q: A solid cylinder starts from rest and rolls without slipping down a height of 0.3 m. Roughly how fast is it at the bottom (g = 9.81 m/s²)?
117349.e: From m · g · h = ¾ · m · v² it follows that v = √(4 · g · h / 3) = √(3.92) ≈ 2.0 m/s. A body sliding without friction would be faster, at about 2.4 m/s.
117349.m: Rolling bodies are slower than sliding ones.

117350.q: A disc with J = 0.5 kg·m² rotates at 600 revolutions per minute. Roughly what is its rotational energy?
117350.e: 600 per minute is 10 per second, so ω = 2π · 10 ≈ 62.8 rad/s. E = ½ · 0.5 · 62.8² ≈ 990 J.
117350.m: First convert rates of rotation into radians per second.

117351.q: Why is the Earth's rotational energy slowly decreasing?
117351.e: The tides caused by the Moon rub against the sea floor and slow the Earth's rotation. As a result, the days are getting longer very slowly.
117351.m: The tides slow the Earth down.

117352.q: In physics, what is meant by a top (gyroscope)?
a: A rigid body rotating about a fixed point
Any body on a circular path
117352.e: A top is a rigid body that can turn about a fixed point. Toy spinning tops are just one example.
117352.m: A top rotates about a fixed point.

117353.q: What is the slow circling movement of the axis of a tilted toy top called?
117353.e: Gravity exerts a torque on the tilted top. Instead of falling over, its axis slowly moves round in a circle. The Earth's axis also precesses, once in about 26,000 years.
117353.m: Precession is the slow circling of a top's axis.

117354.q: Why does a fast-spinning top not fall over straight away?
a: Gravity only changes the direction of its angular momentum
Gravity does not act on it
It floats on the air pressure
It is magnetically fixed to the floor
117354.e: The torque from gravity is perpendicular to the angular momentum. It turns the axis sideways instead of tipping the top over.
117354.m: A fast top moves sideways instead of falling over.

117355.q: In space, a cosmonaut watched a spinning wing nut flip over again and again. What is this effect called?
117355.e: In 1985, Vladimir Dzhanibekov saw in weightlessness that rotation about a certain axis is unstable. The body flips over at regular intervals.
117355.m: The Dzhanibekov effect shows unstable rotation in weightlessness.

117356.q: Which device uses the Earth's rotation and a gyroscope to find north without a magnetic field?
117356.e: In a gyrocompass, the Earth's rotation turns the gyroscope's axis into the north-south direction, that is, into the plane of the meridian. It shows geographic north and is not disturbed by iron.

117357.q: Why are bullets from rifled gun barrels given a spin?
a: The rotation stabilises their direction of flight
117357.e: By spinning about its long axis, the bullet acts like a gyroscope. Its angular momentum stops it from tumbling in flight.

117358.q: After which mathematician from Basel are the equations of motion of a rigid spinning body named?
117358.e: In the 18th century, Leonhard Euler set up Euler's equations for rotating bodies. They describe rotation in a frame of reference that moves with the body.
117358.m: The equations for spinning bodies come from Leonhard Euler.

117359.q: What do you call a top in which two of the three principal moments of inertia are equal?
117359.e: In a symmetric top, two principal moments of inertia are equal and the figure axis is an axis of symmetry. If all three are equal, it is called a spherical top.
117359.m: A symmetric top has two equal principal moments of inertia.

a: The change in direction of an axis of rotation under a torque
A top slowing down because of friction
An increase in the rate of spin
117360.e: If a torque acts on a rotating body at right angles to its angular momentum, the axis traces out the surface of a cone. This movement is called precession.
117360.m: Precession is the wandering of the axis of rotation.

117361.q: Roughly how long does one cycle of the precession of the Earth's axis take?
117361.e: The Earth's axis traces a cone with a period of about 26,000 years. This is also called the Platonic year.
117361.m: The Earth's axis precesses once in about 26,000 years.

117362.q: What effect does the precession of the Earth's axis have on the sky?
a: The pole star changes over thousands of years
The phases of the Moon disappear
The Sun rises in the west
117362.e: The celestial poles slowly move along a circle. In a few thousand years a different bright star will be near the north celestial pole.

117363.q: A tilted top is spinning fast. Why does it not simply tip over, but its axis moves round in a circle instead?
a: The torque from gravity only changes the direction of the angular momentum
The air holds the top up
Gravity does not act on spinning bodies
Friction with the floor lifts it
117363.e: Gravity produces a torque at right angles to the angular momentum. It does not change its size, only its direction, and the axis traces out a cone.
117363.m: A torque pushes the axis of a top sideways.

117364.q: How does the rate of precession of a top change when it spins faster?
117364.e: The rate of precession is inversely proportional to the angular momentum. So a fast top precesses slowly.
117364.m: The faster the top, the slower the precession.

117365.q: Which medical imaging method is based on the precession of nuclear spins in a magnetic field?
117365.e: In a strong magnetic field, the nuclear spins of hydrogen atoms precess at the Larmor frequency. MRI uses the signals from these spins.
117365.m: MRI uses the precession of nuclear spins.

117366.q: Which theory was the first to fully explain the observed precession of Mercury's perihelion?
117366.e: Part of the perihelion precession, about 43 arcseconds per century, could not be explained with Newton. In 1915 Einstein explained it with the general theory of relativity.
117366.m: Mercury's perihelion precession confirmed Einstein's theory.

117367.q: Which two conditions must be met for a rigid body to be in equilibrium?
a: The sum of forces and the sum of torques are zero
Only the sum of forces is zero
117367.e: For a rigid body to be neither shifted nor turned, all forces and all torques must cancel each other out.
117367.m: In equilibrium, forces and torques cancel out.

117368.q: What kind of equilibrium does a ball at the bottom of a bowl have?
117368.e: If the ball is pushed aside, its centre of mass rises. Gravity drives it back to its starting position.
117368.m: In stable equilibrium a body returns to its position.

117369.q: How many independent equilibrium conditions must a freely movable rigid body in space meet?
117369.e: In space there are three components of force and three components of torque. All six sums must be zero.
117369.m: In space a rigid body has six equilibrium conditions.

117370.q: On a mobile rod, a figure of 0.2 kg hangs on the left, 0.3 m from the suspension point. Where must a figure of 0.3 kg hang on the right so that the rod stays level?
117370.e: The torques must be equal: 0.2 · 0.3 = 0.3 · x. It follows that x = 0.06 / 0.3 = 0.2 m.
117370.m: In a mobile the torques balance each other.

117371.q: A child of 30 kg sits on a seesaw 2 m from the pivot. Where must a child of 40 kg sit on the other side for it to balance?
117371.e: The torques must be equal: 30 · 2 = 40 · x. It follows that x = 60 / 40 = 1.5 m.
117371.m: The heavier child sits closer to the pivot.

117372.q: A beam 4 m long weighing 200 N rests on supports at both ends. A load of 600 N hangs 1 m from the left end. What force does the left support carry?
117372.e: Moments about the right support: 200 N · 2 m + 600 N · 3 m = F_L · 4 m. So F_L = 2200 / 4 = 550 N.
117372.m: The support closer to the load carries more.

117373.q: Why does a construction crane carry a heavy counterweight on its short jib?
a: To balance the torque of the load
To make the crane turn faster
117373.e: The load on the long jib produces a large torque about the tower. The counterweight acts on the other side and keeps the overall centre of mass above the base.
117373.m: A counterweight stops the crane from tipping over.

117374.q: Where is a hanging body positioned when it is in stable equilibrium?
a: Its centre of mass is directly below the point of suspension
Its centre of mass is above the point of suspension
Its centre of mass is beside the point of suspension
Its centre of mass is at the point of suspension
117374.e: If the centre of mass hangs below the point of suspension, any displacement lifts it. The weight turns the body back.
117374.m: Hanging bodies come to rest with their centre of mass at the bottom.

117375.q: What does statics, a branch of mechanics, deal with?
117375.e: Statics studies how forces act on bodies and structures at rest. It is the basis for calculating bridges and buildings.
117375.m: Statics studies forces on bodies at rest.

117376.q: Which ancient scholar is said to have said “Give me a place to stand, and I will move the world”?
117376.e: Archimedes formulated the law of the lever. The saying shows that with a long enough lever you could move any load.
117376.m: Archimedes formulated the law of the lever.

117377.q: How many independent equilibrium conditions does a rigid body in a plane have?
117377.e: In a plane there are two force equations, horizontal and vertical, and one moment equation. This lets you work out at most three unknown support forces.
117377.m: In a plane there are three equilibrium conditions.

117378.q: What force can a roller support take in a plane?
a: Only a force perpendicular to the direction it can slide
117378.e: A roller support can move along its track. So it only transmits a force perpendicular to it, for example so that a bridge can expand in the heat.
117378.m: A roller support allows movement along its track.

117379.q: Which drawing method do you use to add two forces acting at the same point?
117379.e: The two force arrows form two sides of a parallelogram. The diagonal is the resultant force.

117380.q: A 50 N lamp hangs in the middle of a rope whose two halves are each tilted at 30° to the horizontal. What is the force in each half of the rope?
117380.e: The vertical parts of both rope forces carry the lamp: 2 · F · sin(30°) = 50 N. With sin(30°) = 0.5, F = 50 N.
117380.m: Ropes stretched flat carry large forces.

117381.q: Which forces occur in the members of an ideal truss?
117381.e: In an ideal truss, the members are joined by hinges and are only loaded at the joints. So only forces along the direction of each member act in them.
117381.m: Truss members are only loaded in tension or compression.

117382.q: A block weighing 100 N rests on a slope inclined at 30°. How large is the force pulling it down the slope?
